accesskeys_review_ACCESSKEY_DUPLICATE_fa: Only one of the elements responds to the key, so the others cannot be reached by their shortcut (best practice, related to WCAG 2.1.1).
accesskeys_review_ACCESSKEY_DUPLICATE_pa: Each element with that key can be reached by it, or the duplicates are intended and harmless.
accesskeys_review_ACCESSKEY_DUPLICATE_st: Note the access key the report names and find the other elements sharing it.
Press the browser's access key combination with that key (for example Alt, or Alt+Shift, plus the key) and note which element is focused or activated.
Press it again and check whether each element sharing the key can be reached.
area_altQuality_review_TEXT_ALTERNATIVE_: The text alternative is wrong, generic, a file name or doesn't say where the link leads, which fails WCAG 1.1.1 (H24).
The text alternative tells the user where the link goes, in words that match the region.
Find the image map area the report names and look at the part of the image it covers.
Click it, or follow its link, and note where it leads.
Read the area's text alternative (and every other source the report lists) and check that it says where the link leads or what the region is.
ariaAllowedAttr_review_ARIA_ATTR_DEPRECA: The state is conveyed only by the deprecated attribute and the screen reader does not announce it, so the element's state is not exposed (WCAG 4.1.2).
The state is announced, or it is also conveyed by a native attribute or a supported role, so nothing depends on the deprecated attribute alone.
Inspect the element the report names and note the deprecated aria-* attribute and the element's role.
Open the Accessibility pane in the browser's developer tools and check whether the attribute's state still shows on the element (for example disabled, invalid, has popup).
With a screen reader, move to the element and listen for that state being announced.
Look for a non-deprecated way to convey the same thing (a native attribute such as disabled, or a role that supports the attribute) and whether the page already uses it.
ariaAllowedRole_review_ARIA_ROLE_NOT_ALL: The announced role contradicts the element's behaviour, such as a focusable button announced as a heading, which fails ARIA in HTML and can fail WCAG 4.1.2.
The announced role matches how the element looks and behaves (or role none/presentation was ignored on a focusable control and its native role is kept).
Inspect the element the report names and note its tag and its role attribute.
Open the Accessibility pane in the browser's developer tools and check which role is exposed.
Press Tab to see whether the element takes keyboard focus, and try operating it with Enter or Space if it is a control.
With a screen reader, move to the element and compare what is announced with what the element does on screen.
ariaBrailleEquivalent_review_BRAILLE_ATT: A control or image has only a braille label, so speech users get no name, which fails WCAG 4.1.2.
The element has a spoken name (and a roledescription where a braille one is given), or its role needs no name and nothing is lost.
Inspect the element the report names and note whether it has aria-braillelabel or aria-brailleroledescription.
If it has aria-braillelabel, open the Accessibility pane in the browser's developer tools and read the element's accessible name.
If the role is one that needs a name (button, link, image, checkbox and similar), confirm that a name exists besides the braille label; with a screen reader in speech, listen for it.
If it has aria-brailleroledescription, check whether it also has aria-roledescription; if not, confirm the native role is still announced and nothing else was meant.
ariaCheckedStateMismatch_review_ARIA_CHE: Assistive technology reports a different state from the one shown, which fails WCAG 4.1.2.
The state assistive technology reports matches what the control shows, before and after it is changed.
Wait until the page has fully loaded, then find the checkbox or radio button the report names and note whether it looks checked.
Open the Accessibility pane and read its checked state.
Click it, or press Space, and check that both the look and the state in the Accessibility pane change together, or listen with a screen reader.
ariaConditionalAttr_review_ARIA_ERRORMES: Error text is visible but aria-invalid stays absent or false, and the screen reader announces the message neither on the field nor when it appears, which fails WCAG 3.3.1 / 4.1.2 (see ARIA21).

When the error is shown, the screen reader announces it, either on the field (aria-invalid="true" or the message in aria-describedby) or as soon as it appears; when no error is shown, nothing needs exposing.
Inspect the field the report names and note the id in its aria-errormessage.
Enter an invalid value (or leave a required field empty) and submit or leave the field, so any error appears.
Look whether the element with that id now shows error text, and inspect the field again for aria-invalid="true".
With a screen reader, move back to the field and listen for the error message.

If you don't hear the error on the field, check whether the page reads it out another way, for example as soon as the message appears, without you moving focus. It only counts if the screen reader announces the whole message.
ariaDeprecatedRole_review_ARIA_ROLE_AUTH: role="generic" strips a native meaning, such as a link or heading no longer announced as one, which fails WCAG 4.1.2 (and 1.3.1 for structure).
The element was already a generic container, or its native role still shows and is announced.
Inspect the element the report names and note its tag and role="generic".
If the tag is a plain container (div, span, b, i), the role changes nothing; remove it as cleanup.
Otherwise open the Accessibility pane in the browser's developer tools and check whether the element's native meaning (button, link, heading, list item, navigation) has been lost.
With a screen reader, move to the element and, if it is focusable, press Tab to it and listen to what is announced.
ariaDeprecatedRole_review_ARIA_ROLE_DEPR: The structure is not conveyed by assistive technology because it relies on the deprecated role, which can fail WCAG 4.1.2.
The structure is announced correctly (for example as a list with its item count), or the role is replaced with the suggested one.
Inspect the element the report names and note its deprecated role (such as directory).
Open the Accessibility pane in the browser's developer tools and check which role is exposed (directory is usually mapped to list).
With a screen reader, move to the element and its items and listen for the structure being announced.
Consider the suggested replacement role (list for directory) and whether it fits.
ariaExpandedStateMismatch_review_EXPANDE: The content is fully shown while the toggle tells screen reader users it is collapsed, which fails WCAG 4.1.2.
The content is collapsed or only previewed while the toggle says collapsed, and the state changes when the content opens.
Find the toggle the report names; it says it is collapsed.
Look at the content it controls and check whether it is shown in full or only a preview, such as a few clamped lines.
Activate the toggle with Enter or Space and check the Accessibility pane: the expanded state should follow what is shown.
The content stays hidden while the toggle tells screen reader users it is expanded, which fails WCAG 4.1.2.
The content is shown while the toggle says expanded, once any transition ends.
Find the toggle the report names; it says it is expanded.
Look for the content it controls and check whether it is shown on screen, waiting for any animation to finish.
Activate the toggle with Enter or Space and check in the Accessibility pane that the expanded state follows what is shown.
ariaHidden_focus_review_ariaHiddenFocusa: Focus reaches content behind the dialog inside aria-hidden="true", where a screen reader announces nothing, which fails WCAG 4.1.2.
Focus stays inside the open dialog and never reaches the hidden content behind it.
Find the element the report names, behind the modal dialog open on the page, and note what in it can take focus.
With the dialog open, press Tab repeatedly, then Shift+Tab, and watch where focus goes.
Whenever focus seems to leave the dialog, check document.activeElement in the developer tools console.
Focus can stay on the element inside aria-hidden="true", where a screen reader announces nothing, which fails WCAG 4.1.2.
Focus never stays on the hidden element: it passes straight on to a visible control, as a focus trap's sentinel does.
Click just before the element the report names, then press Tab until focus should reach it.
Watch where focus lands and check document.activeElement in the developer tools console.
Press Shift+Tab from the control after it and see whether focus stops on the hidden element or passes straight on.
ariaProhibitedAttr_review_ARIA_ATTR_PROH: The label carries information given nowhere else (such as "Price in euros" on "12" with no header saying so), which is lost because naming is not supported on an element with no role (WCAG 4.1.2, ACT kb1m8s).
The visible text, or text a screen reader reads with it such as its table header, already says everything the label says, so nothing is lost if the label is ignored.
Inspect the element the report names and note its aria-label or aria-labelledby text and its visible text.
Compare the two: check whether the label says anything the visible text does not.
If it does, check whether that information is given another way that a screen reader also reads, such as a table header above the cell or text next to the element.
With a screen reader, read the element in browse mode and note whether the label is announced or ignored.
ariaRequiredAttr_review_ARIA_ATTR_REQUIR: The announced value is wrong, such as a combobox announced collapsed while its list is open or a level 2 heading that should be another level, which fails WCAG 4.1.2 (or 1.3.1 for headings).
The default value matches reality: the combobox reports collapsed only when its popup is closed, or the heading really is level 2.
Inspect the element the report names and note its role and the missing attribute (such as aria-expanded on a combobox, aria-level on a heading).
For a combobox, open and close its popup with the keyboard (Alt+Down Arrow, Escape) and the mouse, and check whether aria-expanded is added and updated.
For a heading, compare its place in the page outline with level 2, the default it gets, and check whether a different level is meant.
With a screen reader, move to the element and listen for the state or level announced.
ariaRequiredAttr_review_state_internals_: The required state is missing from the accessibility tree or does not change when the element is used, which fails WCAG 4.1.2.
The state is exposed and updates as the element is used, set through its internals.
Inspect the custom element the report names and note its role and the missing state (such as checked or value).
Open the Accessibility pane in the browser's developer tools and check whether that state shows for the element.
Operate the element (click it, press Space or the arrow keys) and check whether the state shown in the pane changes.
With a screen reader, move to the element and listen for the state.
ariaRequiredChildren_review_ARIA_REQUIRE: It shows items (images, icons, controls) that lack the required child role, so the structure is not conveyed, which fails WCAG 1.3.1 (ACT bc4a75).
The container is empty and conveys nothing, or the items it shows carry the required role.
Inspect the container the report names and note its role and the child roles it needs (such as listitem for list, option for listbox).
Look at what it shows on screen: check whether it is empty or holds images, icons or controls.
Interact with the page (open menus, load results) and check whether children with the required role are added later.
Open the Accessibility pane in the browser's developer tools and check the roles of anything it holds.
ariaRoleNamePresent_review_name_internal: The element has no name in the accessibility tree and the screen reader announces only its role, which fails WCAG 4.1.2.
The accessibility tree shows a name for the element, set through its internals or otherwise, and the screen reader announces it.
Inspect the custom element the report names and note its role.
Open the Accessibility pane in the browser's developer tools and read the element's accessible name.
With a screen reader, move to the element and listen to the name announced.
ariaRolesValid_review_ARIA_ROLE_ABSTRACT: The native role does not match the intent (such as a button marked landmark), so the meant role is never exposed, which fails WCAG 4.1.2 (ACT 674b10).
The native role is a concrete form of what the author named, so the element is still exposed correctly (still remove the abstract role).
Inspect the element the report names and note the abstract role (such as landmark, widget, command) and its tag.
Open the Accessibility pane in the browser's developer tools and check the role exposed instead (the native role).
Decide whether the native role is a concrete kind of the abstract role named (a nav for landmark, a button for widget).
ariaRolesValid_review_ARIA_ROLE_INVALID_: The intended role differs from the exposed one, so users get the wrong role, which fails WCAG 4.1.2 (ACT 674b10).
The exposed native role is the one that was meant, so users get the right role (still correct the typo).
Inspect the element the report names and note the unknown role value and its tag.
Work out which role was probably meant (for example "buton" for button).
Open the Accessibility pane in the browser's developer tools and check the role that is exposed instead (the element's native role).
Compare the exposed role with the intended one and with how the element behaves.
ariaText_review_ROLE_TEXT_HAS_FOCUSABLE_: The focusable element is announced as plain text, or not at all, so users can't tell it is interactive (best practice, WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices).
The focusable element is announced with its role and name and can be used, or it doesn't need to be focusable.
Inspect the element the report names and find the focusable element inside it.
Press Tab until that element has focus, with a screen reader running, and listen to what is announced.
Try to activate it with Enter or Space.
ariaValidAttrValue_review_ARIA_ACTIVEDES: The screen reader announces nothing or the wrong item as the active one changes, so keyboard users cannot follow it, which fails WCAG 4.1.2.
Each active item is announced as the arrow keys move through it.
Inspect the element the report names and note the id in its aria-activedescendant and where that element sits.
Focus the element and use the arrow keys to move the active item.
With a screen reader running, listen whether each active item is announced as you move.
Check whether the referenced element could be moved inside the element or tied to it with aria-owns or aria-controls.
ariaValidAttrValue_review_ARIA_ATTR_VALU: The id never resolves (missing, misspelled, or across a shadow boundary) and nothing else gives the label, description or relation, so it is lost, which fails WCAG 4.1.2 (ACT 6a7281).
The referenced element exists when it matters and the name, description or relation shows in the accessibility tree, or the element gets the same name or description another way.
Inspect the element the report names and note the attribute and the ids it refers to.
Use the page as a user would (open, expand, submit) to reach the state where the referenced element should exist.
In the developer tools console, run document.getElementById('the-id') for each id and check for a near-miss id in the markup (different case, typo, or inside another shadow root).
Open the Accessibility pane in the browser's developer tools and check whether the name, description or relation it should supply appears.
If it does not appear, check in the Accessibility pane whether the element still gets that name or description another way, for example from its own text, a <label> or an aria-label.
ariaValidAttrValue_review_ARIA_HASPOPUP_: The popup that opens has another role than announced (such as a dialog announced as a menu), misleading screen reader users, which fails WCAG 4.1.2.
The popup that opens has the role aria-haspopup announces.
Inspect the element the report names and note its aria-haspopup value (menu, listbox, tree, grid, dialog; true means menu).
Open the popup with the mouse and with the keyboard (Enter, Space or Down Arrow).
Inspect the popup that appears and check its role in the Accessibility pane in the browser's developer tools.
Compare the popup's role with the type aria-haspopup announces.
ariaValidAttr_review_ARIA_ATTR_INVALID_f: It is a typo of a real attribute and its effect is missing, such as a control with no name or decorative content not hidden, which fails WCAG 4.1.2 (ACT 5f99a7).
ariaValidAttr_review_ARIA_ATTR_INVALID_p: The attribute is a data hook not meant for assistive technology, or what it meant is supplied another way.
ariaValidAttr_review_ARIA_ATTR_INVALID_s: Inspect the element the report names and note the unknown aria-* attribute.
Check whether it is a misspelling of a real one (aria-lable, aria-labeledby, aria-describeby, aria-hiden) or a made-up hook (aria-qa, aria-test).
If it is a misspelling, open the Accessibility pane in the browser's developer tools and check whether what the real attribute would give (name, description, hidden state) is present anyway.
With a screen reader, move to the element and listen to what is announced.
avoidInlineSpacing_review_INLINE_SPACING: The forced value is below the metric on wrapping text and the text cannot take user spacing without loss, which fails WCAG 1.4.12.
The forced value meets the WCAG 1.4.12 metric, or the text does not wrap, or nothing is lost with the spacing applied.
Inspect the element the report names and read the !important spacing value in its style attribute.
In the Computed tab of the developer tools, read the resulting line-height, letter-spacing or word-spacing in pixels and compare with 1.5 times, 0.12 times or 0.16 times the font size.

Apply the WCAG 1.4.12 text spacing (line-height 1.5, letter-spacing 0.12em, word-spacing 0.16em, paragraph spacing 2em) with !important, for example through a user stylesheet or a bookmarklet; since the element's own !important inline style wins, also note the values it keeps.
Narrow to 320 CSS pixels and check whether the text is cut off or overlaps.
The text does wrap and, with the forced spacing, lines overlap or text is clipped, which fails WCAG 1.4.12.
The text cannot wrap (it stays on one line or scrolls) and nothing is cut off or overlaps, so the criterion does not apply.
Inspect the element the report names and note which spacing property its style attribute forces with !important.
Narrow the window to 320 CSS pixels wide (or zoom to 400%) and check whether the text ever wraps onto a second line.

Apply the WCAG 1.4.12 text spacing (line-height 1.5, letter-spacing 0.12em, word-spacing 0.16em, paragraph spacing 2em) with !important, for example through a user stylesheet or a bookmarklet; since the element's own !important inline style wins, also note the values it keeps.
Check whether any text is cut off, overlaps or is hidden.
The text wraps and the forced spacing makes lines overlap or text clip, which fails WCAG 1.4.12.
The text stays on one line at every width, or wraps without lines overlapping or text being lost.
Inspect the element the report names and note which spacing property its style attribute forces with !important.
Narrow the window to 320 CSS pixels wide (or zoom to 400%) and check whether the short text wraps onto two lines.

Apply the WCAG 1.4.12 text spacing (line-height 1.5, letter-spacing 0.12em, word-spacing 0.16em, paragraph spacing 2em) with !important, for example through a user stylesheet or a bookmarklet; since the element's own !important inline style wins, also note the values it keeps.
Check whether the text is cut off, overlaps or is hidden.
binaryControlNamePresent_review_name_int: The control has no name in the accessibility tree and the screen reader announces only its role, which fails WCAG 4.1.2.
The accessibility tree shows a name for the control, set through its internals or otherwise, and the screen reader announces it.
Inspect the control the report names, a custom element, and note its role.
Open the Accessibility pane in the browser's developer tools and read the element's accessible name.
With a screen reader, move to the element and listen to the name announced.
buttonNamePresent_review_name_closedCont: The button has no name in the accessibility tree, since its content gives none, which fails WCAG 4.1.2.
The accessibility tree shows a name for the button, taken from its content, and the screen reader announces it.
Find the button the report names and note the text or icon it shows on screen.
Open the Accessibility pane in the browser's developer tools and read the element's accessible name, which the browser works out from content no script can read.
With a screen reader, move to the element and listen to the name announced.
buttonNamePresent_review_name_contentToo: The button has no name in the accessibility tree, since its content gives none, which fails WCAG 4.1.2.
The accessibility tree shows a name for the button, taken from its nested content, and the screen reader announces it.
Find the button the report names and note the text it shows on screen.
Open the Accessibility pane in the browser's developer tools and read the element's accessible name, which the browser works out from all of its nested content.
With a screen reader, move to the element and listen to the name announced.
buttonNamePresent_review_name_internals_: The button has no name in the accessibility tree and the screen reader announces only its role, which fails WCAG 4.1.2.
The accessibility tree shows a name for the button, set through its internals or otherwise, and the screen reader announces it.
Inspect the button the report names, a custom element, and note its role.
Open the Accessibility pane in the browser's developer tools and read the element's accessible name.
With a screen reader, move to the element and listen to the name announced.
bypassBlocksPresent_review_BYPASS_MECHAN: Repeated blocks have no way to skip them, so keyboard and screen reader users must go through them on every page, which fails WCAG 2.4.1.
The page has no repeated blocks, or offers a working skip link, a main landmark or headings that let users jump past them.
Close any dialog or overlay, then look at whether the page repeats blocks such as a header or menu that appear on other pages of the site.
Click the address bar and press Tab: check whether a skip link appears that moves focus past the repeated blocks to the main content.
Check for headings at the start of the main content, or a main landmark, in the Accessibility pane or by a screen reader's headings and landmarks lists.
canvas_textAltQuality_review_TEXT_ALTERN: Neither the text alternative nor a description reachable from it gives the information the canvas shows, or the text is vague or wrong, which fails WCAG 1.1.1.
The text alternative, alone or with a description a screen reader user can reach from it, gives the same information or purpose as what the canvas shows.
Look at what the canvas the report names shows on screen, including any changes as you use it.
Read its text alternative (the value the report gives, or its fallback content and name in the Accessibility pane).

If the text alternative only names the canvas, as is common for charts and diagrams, the details may be given elsewhere: in a caption, text or a table next to it, or a link beside it. That counts only if a screen reader user can find it from the canvas and it gives everything the canvas shows.
Check that the text, with any such description, conveys the same information or purpose as the drawing, and keeps up if the drawing changes.
clickHandlerKeyboardOperable_review_CLIC: Pressing Enter or Space does nothing even after focus arrives, and what the click does cannot be done another way with the keyboard, which fails WCAG 2.1.1 (F54).
Enter (and Space for button-like controls) does what a click does, or, for a tab, moving focus to it already shows its panel, or what the click does can be done another way with the keyboard alone.
Click the element the report names and note what happens.
Reload, then press Tab until the element has focus.
Press Enter, then Space, and compare with what the click did.

If the keyboard can't do it here, check whether what the click does can be done another way with the keyboard alone, for example with a button or menu item elsewhere on the page. It only counts if it does everything the click does.
Pressing Enter or Space does nothing on the element, so the listener above does not handle it, and what the click does cannot be done another way with the keyboard, which fails WCAG 2.1.1.
Enter (and Space for button-like controls) does what a click does, or what the click does can be done another way with the keyboard alone.
Click the element the report names and note what happens.
Press Tab until the element has focus.
Press Enter, then Space (and the arrow keys if it sits in a group), and compare with the click.

If the keyboard can't do it here, check whether what the click does can be done another way with the keyboard alone, for example with a button or menu item elsewhere on the page. It only counts if it does everything the click does.
The action can only be done with a mouse, which fails WCAG 2.1.1 (F54, F42).
The same action can be done by keyboard, through the managing widget or another control.
Click the element the report names and note what its click does.
Press Tab through the page and check that the element never takes focus.
If it is an item in a list, grid or combobox, focus that widget and use the arrow keys to see whether the item becomes active and Enter performs the action.
Otherwise look for another keyboard-operable control on the page that does the same thing.
No key moves focus to the element and what the click does cannot be done another way with the keyboard, so its action is mouse-only, which fails WCAG 2.1.1.
The element can be reached by keyboard (Tab or arrow keys within its group) and Enter or Space does what a click does, or what the click does can be done another way with the keyboard alone.
Click the element the report names and note what happens.
Press Tab through the page and check whether focus ever lands on it.
If it is part of a group (tabs, menu, toolbar, list), Tab into the group and use the arrow keys to see whether they move focus to it.
Once it has focus, press Enter or Space and compare with the click.

If the keyboard can't do it here, check whether what the click does can be done another way with the keyboard alone, for example with a button or menu item elsewhere on the page. It only counts if it does everything the click does.
Pressing Enter or Space does nothing, or less than a click, and what the click does cannot be done another way with the keyboard, which fails WCAG 2.1.1 (F54).
Enter (and Space for button-like controls) does what a click does, or what the click does can be done another way with the keyboard alone.
Click the element the report names and note what happens.
Reload, then press Tab until the element has focus.
Press Enter, then Space, and compare with what the click did.

If the keyboard can't do it here, check whether what the click does can be done another way with the keyboard alone, for example with a button or menu item elsewhere on the page. It only counts if it does everything the click does.
comboboxNamePresent_review_name_internal: The combobox has no name in the accessibility tree and the screen reader announces only its role, which fails WCAG 4.1.2.
The accessibility tree shows a name for the combobox, set through its internals or otherwise, and the screen reader announces it.
Inspect the combobox the report names, a custom element, and note its role.
Open the Accessibility pane in the browser's developer tools and read the element's accessible name.
With a screen reader, move to the element and listen to the name announced.
contrastComputable_review_ANCESTOR_OPACI: The faded colors on screen give a ratio below the threshold, which fails WCAG 1.4.3 (or 1.4.6), unless the text is part of an inactive control.
The faded colors on screen reach the threshold, or the faded text is an inactive (disabled) control, which is exempt.
Find the text the report names and note the ancestor with opacity below 1.

Use the color picker in the browser's developer tools, or a contrast calculator with colors picked by an eyedropper, to measure the text and background as they appear on screen (faded), with an eyedropper on the rendered page.
Compare the ratio with 4.5:1 (3:1 for large text) for WCAG 1.4.3, and 7:1 (4.5:1 for large text) for 1.4.6.
contrastComputable_review_BACKGROUND_FIL: With the filter applied, the ratio on screen falls below the threshold, which fails WCAG 1.4.3 (or 1.4.6).
With the filter applied, the ratio on screen reaches the threshold.
Find the text the report names and note the filter or backdrop-filter on it or an ancestor (in the developer tools Styles pane).

Use the color picker in the browser's developer tools, or a contrast calculator with colors picked by an eyedropper, to measure the text and background colors as they appear on screen with the filter applied, using an eyedropper on the rendered page rather than the declared values.
For a blur or backdrop-filter over changing content, scroll or wait so different content passes behind, and check the worst case.
Compare the ratio with 4.5:1 (3:1 for large text) for WCAG 1.4.3, and 7:1 (4.5:1 for large text) for 1.4.6.
contrastComputable_review_BACKGROUND_IMA: Some part of the background behind the text gives a ratio below the threshold, which fails WCAG 1.4.3 (or 1.4.6).
Every part of the background behind the letters gives at least the threshold ratio.
Find the text the report names and look at the image or gradient behind it.

Use the color picker in the browser's developer tools, or a contrast calculator with colors picked by an eyedropper, to measure the text color against the lightest and darkest parts of the background directly behind the letters.
If the image changes (slides, video, responsive images), check each version and at a few window widths.
Compare the ratio with 4.5:1 (3:1 for large text) for WCAG 1.4.3, and 7:1 (4.5:1 for large text) for 1.4.6.
contrastComputable_review_BACKGROUND_NOT: The ratio is below the threshold anywhere behind the text, which fails WCAG 1.4.3 (or 1.4.6).
The ratio reaches the threshold everywhere behind the text.
Find the text the report names on the page.

Use the color picker in the browser's developer tools, or a contrast calculator with colors picked by an eyedropper, to measure the text color against the color seen directly behind the letters, taking the darkest and lightest points if it varies.
Compare the ratio with 4.5:1 (3:1 for large text) for WCAG 1.4.3, and 7:1 (4.5:1 for large text) for 1.4.6.
In some setting where the page is shown the ratio is below the threshold, which fails WCAG 1.4.3 (or 1.4.6).
The ratio reaches the threshold in every setting where the page is shown.
Find the text the report names; the page sets no opaque background behind it, so what shows there is the canvas the browser paints, or, in a frame, the page around it.
View the page where it is shown: inside the page that embeds it, with forced colors off, and in each color scheme the page supports (light and dark).
Use the color picker in the browser's developer tools, or a contrast calculator with colors picked by an eyedropper, to measure the text against the background actually seen in each setting.
Compare the ratio with 4.5:1 (3:1 for large text) for WCAG 1.4.3, and 7:1 (4.5:1 for large text) for 1.4.6.
contrastComputable_review_BACKGROUND_OVE: The color actually behind the text gives a ratio below the threshold, which fails WCAG 1.4.3 (or 1.4.6).
The color actually behind the text gives at least the threshold ratio.
Find the text the report names and check which element actually paints behind it (inspect it and toggle the overlapping element off and on).
Use the color picker in the browser's developer tools, or a contrast calculator with colors picked by an eyedropper, to measure the text color against the color actually seen behind the letters.
Compare the ratio with 4.5:1 (3:1 for large text) for WCAG 1.4.3, and 7:1 (4.5:1 for large text) for 1.4.6.

Watch the focus indicator and check document.activeElement in the developer tools console.
Try to operate the element with the keyboard (type, press Enter or Space).
A visible control sends focus elsewhere as it arrives, so it cannot be reached or operated by keyboard, which fails WCAG 2.1.1 and 2.4.7 (F55).
Focus goes to a sensible place (a dialog's focus wrap) or stays on the element, and every control can still be reached and operated by keyboard.
Read the onfocus handler the report quotes and note which element it sends focus to.
Click just before the element, then press Tab until focus should reach it, and see where focus lands (check document.activeElement in the console).
If the element is an invisible, unnamed sentinel at the edge of a dialog that wraps focus back inside, note that this is a focus trap for a modal and expected.
Otherwise, try to operate the element with the keyboard and press Shift+Tab to see whether you can go back.
focusOrderSemantics_review_TABBABLE_WITH: The element acts as a control (it opens, toggles or navigates) but is announced with a non-interactive role such as heading or list, so keyboard users are not told what it does; a best-practice miss related to WCAG 4.1.2. If it does nothing and does not scroll, it is a needless tab stop.
The element is focusable for a reason its role supports, such as a scrollable region a keyboard user needs to scroll, and does not act as a control.
Press Tab until focus reaches the element the report names and listen with a screen reader, or read its role in the Accessibility pane.
Find out why it is focusable: does it scroll (its content overflows and arrow keys scroll it), or does it do something when clicked or when Enter or Space is pressed?
If it acts as a control, compare the announced role with what it does.
formControlLabelQuality_review_DUPLICATE: Different fields share a label and nothing visible tells them apart, so a user cannot tell which to fill in, which fails WCAG 2.4.6 (G131).
The fields serve the same purpose, or something visible near each one makes clear which is which.
Find the field the report names and the other fields with the same visible label.
Look at the screen around each one: a legend, heading, row text or nearby text that says which is which.
Decide whether the fields ask for the same thing (a repeated search box) or different things (shipping and billing name).
formControlLabelQuality_review_PARTIALLY: Neither the visible part of the label nor anything visible around it identifies the field without the hidden part (for example, only "Go" is shown), which fails WCAG 2.4.6 (ACT cc0f0a).
The visible part of the label, alone or with what is visible around it, describes the field; the hidden part only adds detail.
Find the field the report names and read its visible label on screen.
Inspect the field in the Accessibility pane and read its full computed name, including the hidden parts.
Look at what is visible around the field, such as a group title, a heading, or the row or column it sits in, which can give the hidden part its meaning.
Ask whether the visible label, read with what is visible around it, tells a sighted user what to enter or choose.
formControlLabelQuality_review_PLACEHOLD: The label is placeholder text that does not say what the field is for, which fails WCAG 2.4.6 (G131).
The label is a real name for what the field asks for in this context (for example "Value" in a key/value editor).
Find the field the report names and read its visible label.
Work out from the page what the field is for.
Decide whether the label says that, or is template text such as "Label", "Field" or "Enter text".
formControlSingleLabel_review_FORM_FIELD: The field gets no name or an incomplete one because of the empty label, which fails WCAG 3.3.2 (and 4.1.2).
The field's name is the text of the real label, and nothing is lost to the empty one.
Find the field the report names and note its label with text and the empty label also pointing at it.
Open the Accessibility pane in the browser's developer tools and check that the field's name is the text of the real label.
With a screen reader, Tab to the field and listen to the name.
The joined name is confusing or misleading, such as two unrelated labels run together, which fails WCAG 3.3.2 (and can fail 2.5.3 and 4.1.2).
The joined name is clear: the labels repeat each other or the extra one is only a marker such as "required".
Find the field the report names and note the text of each label pointing at it.
Open the Accessibility pane in the browser's developer tools and read the field's accessible name, which joins all the labels.
With a screen reader, Tab to the field and listen to the name.
Decide whether the joined name still says clearly what to enter.
formControl_programmaticLabelQuality_rev: Nothing shown on screen tells what to enter in the field, which fails WCAG 3.3.2.
Text shown next to the field, or an icon whose meaning is plain such as a magnifier on a search field, tells what to enter.
Find the field the report names on screen and read its aria-label, which the report gives.
Look for text shown next to the field (a visible label, a heading or a legend) that tells what to enter.
The label is only in hidden elements and nothing on screen tells what to enter, which fails WCAG 3.3.2.
The labelling text is shown with the field, or other text next to it, or a button right after it such as Search, tells what to enter.
Find the field the report names and, in the developer tools, follow its aria-labelledby ids to the elements they point at.
Check whether those elements are shown on screen when the field is.
Look for other text shown next to the field that tells what to enter. A button right after the field that says what it does, such as Search after a search field, also counts.
Once the field is filled in, nothing on screen tells what it is for, which fails WCAG 3.3.2.
A label, text next to the field, or a button right after it such as Search stays on screen once the field is filled in and tells what to enter.
Find the field the report names and read its placeholder.

Check whether anything still shown on screen tells what the field is for: a label or text next to it. A button right after the field that says what it does, such as Search after a search field, also counts.
What to enter is told only by the title, shown on mouse hover, so keyboard and touch users never see it, which fails WCAG 3.3.2.
Without hovering, text next to the field, or a button right after it such as Search, tells what to enter.
Look at the field the report names without hovering over it.
Look for text shown next to it that tells what to enter. A button right after the field that says what it does, such as Search after a search field, also counts.
Tab to the field with the keyboard and note that its title tooltip does not appear.
headingOrder_review_HEADING_ORDER_SKIPPE: The heading jumps more than one level deeper than the one before it (an h2 followed by an h4), leaving a gap in the outline, a best-practice miss (G141).
Each heading is at most one level deeper than the heading before it, so the outline has no gap.
Find the heading the report names and note its level and the previous heading's level (from the report or the Accessibility pane).
List the page's headings in order, with a screen reader's headings list or by inspecting them, and look at the section around the skip.
Decide whether the heading belongs one level below the previous heading, or whether a level is missing.
headingQuality_review_FILENAME_LIKE_HEAD: The heading is a leftover file name (such as IMG_1234.jpg) that does not describe the content after it, which fails WCAG 2.4.6 (G130).
The file name is the real subject of the section, such as the document it offers.
Find the heading the report names and read its text.
Read the content that follows it, up to the next heading.
Decide whether that file is the subject of the section (a file offered for download) or a leftover name such as an image's file name.
headingQuality_review_PLACEHOLDER_HEADIN: The heading is placeholder text that does not describe the content after it, which fails WCAG 2.4.6 (G130).
The heading names the topic of the content after it (a numbered "Step 1" over the first step is fine).
Find the heading the report names and read its text.
Read the content that follows it, up to the next heading.
Decide whether the heading describes that content or is template text such as "Heading", "Lorem ipsum" or "Untitled".
headingQuality_review_URL_LIKE_HEADING_f: The address does not describe the content after it, which fails WCAG 2.4.6 (G130).
headingQuality_review_URL_LIKE_HEADING_p: The address is the topic of the section, so it describes the content after it.
headingQuality_review_URL_LIKE_HEADING_s: Find the heading the report names and read its text.
Read the content that follows it, up to the next heading.
Decide whether the web address is the subject of that section (a site being reviewed or listed) or stands in for a real title.
identicalIframesSamePurpose_review_IFRAM: The frames embed different content under the same name (such as two different videos both titled "YouTube video player"), so users cannot tell them apart, which fails WCAG 4.1.2 (ACT 4b1c6c).
The frames serve the same purpose, so sharing a name is fine.
Find the frames the report names and note the shared accessible name (usually their title).
Look at what each frame shows and at its src address.
Decide whether they do the same job (the same map or widget, with only tracking parameters differing) or different ones (two different videos).
The frames show different content under the same name, so users cannot tell them apart, which fails WCAG 4.1.2 (ACT 4b1c6c).
The frames serve the same purpose, so sharing a name is fine.
Find the frames the report names and note the shared accessible name.
Scroll each frame into view so any lazy-loaded content loads, then inspect it for its src, data-src or srcdoc.
Compare what each frame shows and decide whether they do the same job.
identicalLinksSamePurpose_review_SAME_NA: Links with the same name, such as "Read more", lead to pages with different purposes and nothing on the page lets their names tell them apart, which fails WCAG 2.4.9 (ACT b20e66).
Every link with this name leads to the same page or to pages that serve the same purpose, or a setting you can turn on with the keyboard makes each link name say where it leads.
Find all links with the name the report gives (a screen reader's links list helps) and note where each leads.
Open each link and compare the pages it reaches.
Decide whether the pages serve the same purpose (the same page with tracking parameters, or equivalent pages) or different ones.

If they lead to different kinds of pages, check whether the page offers a way to make link names say more, such as a setting that shows the full link text. It only counts if you can turn it on with the keyboard and, with it on, every link name says where it leads.
iframeFocusableContent_review_IFRAME_TAB: A real link or control inside the frame cannot be reached or used with the keyboard because focus skips or bounces away from it, which fails WCAG 2.1.1.
The only focusable element inside the frame is an empty focus guard that sends focus on, and nothing a user needs inside the frame is left out of keyboard reach.
Click on the page just before the frame the report names, then press Tab to move toward it.
Keep pressing Tab and watch whether focus ever lands inside the frame, and where it goes when it would arrive there.
Inspect the focusable element inside the frame in the Elements panel: note whether it is an empty focus guard or a real link or control with content.
If it is a real link or control, try every other keyboard route to it (Shift+Tab, the frame's own controls) to see if it can be reached and used.
imageRedundantAlt_review_IMAGE_ALT_REDUN: The image's alt repeats the text beside it, so the same words are read twice, a best-practice miss (H2).
The words are read once: the image is hidden or has alt="", or its alt adds something the text does not say.
Find the image the report names and the text next to it in the same link, button or parent.
With a screen reader, move to that link or button, or read its computed name in the Accessibility pane, and listen to whether the words are said twice.
If the image is already hidden from assistive technology, note that nothing is repeated.
imagesOfText_review_IMAGE_BUTTON_TEXT_RE: The button shows its label as text in an image that could be real text, which fails WCAG 1.4.5.
The image holds no text, only an icon or picture, or the text is a logo or otherwise essential.
Find the image button the report names and look at the image.
Check whether the image contains words or letters, not only an icon.
If it does, decide whether that text could be real text styled with CSS, or whether its look is essential (a logo).
imagesOfText_review_SVG_IMAGE_TEXT_REVIE: The image draws text that could be real text and is not a logo, which fails WCAG 1.4.5.
The text is a logo or its look is essential (or it is only incidental, such as a chart's axis numbers).
Find the image the report names and look at the text drawn in it.
Decide whether it is a logo or wordmark, or text such as a heading, sentence or label.
If it is not a logo, decide whether the text could be real text styled with CSS, or whether its look is essential.
img_altDecorative_review_EXCLUDED_ELEMEN: The image conveys information that nothing else on the page gives, yet it is hidden from assistive technology, which fails WCAG 1.1.1.
The image is purely decorative (a spacer, divider, ornament or a picture whose content the text already gives), so hiding it loses nothing.
Find the image, svg or canvas the report names and look at it on the page.
Ask what a user would miss if it were removed: information, a label, a chart's data, or nothing.
If it conveys something, check whether nearby visible text already says the same thing.
img_altDecorative_review_IMAGE_ONLY_CONT: The control is announced with no name, or only its address, because its sole image is hidden, which fails WCAG 1.1.1 (F89).
The control is still announced with a name that says what it does.
Find the link or button the report names; its only content is a hidden image.
Read the control's computed name in the Accessibility pane, or move to it with a screen reader and listen.
Compare what is announced with what the control does.
img_altQuality_review_IMAGE_ONLY_CONTROL: The alt text does not say what the control does, for example a file name, address, generic word or symbols, which fails WCAG 1.1.1 (H30, F30).
The alt text states the control's purpose or destination.
Find the link or button the report names; the image is its only content, so its alt is the control's name.
Read the alt text, then activate the control or check its destination to learn what it does.
Decide whether the alt says what the control does ("Search", "Home"), not what the image looks like.
img_altQuality_review_TEXT_ALTERNATIVE_R: Neither the alt text nor a description reachable from the image conveys the image's content (for example the alt is a file name, address or generic word), which fails WCAG 1.1.1 (F30).
The alt text conveys what the image shows that a user needs, or it names the image and a description a screen reader user can reach from it gives the rest.
Find the image the report names and read its alt text (the report gives the reason it looked suspect, if any).
Look at the image and its context, and ask what it shows that matters to the page.

If the text alternative only names the image, as is common for charts and diagrams, the details may be given elsewhere: in a caption, text or a table next to it, or a link beside it. That counts only if a screen reader user can find it from the image and it gives everything the image shows.
Decide whether the alt says what matters, or names the image while that description gives the rest; a file name, web address or generic word such as "image" does neither.
inputImage_altDecorative_review_NAME_FRO: The name does not say what the button does, for example a file name, address or generic word, which fails WCAG 1.1.1 (H36, F30).
The name states the button's action, such as "Submit order" or "Search".
Find the image button the report names and read its computed name in the Accessibility pane (it comes from aria-label, aria-labelledby or title).
Press the button or read the form to learn what it does.
Decide whether the name says what the button does.
inputImage_altPresent_review_default_nam: The name does not say what the button does (such as "Submit Query" on a search button), which fails WCAG 1.1.1.
The name says what the button does, as "Submit" does on a button that sends a form.
Find the image button the report names and read the name the report gives ("Submit" or "Submit Query").
Look at its image and work out what the button does, for example by what happens when it is pressed.
Decide whether the name says what the button does.
inputImage_altQuality_review_TEXT_ALTERN: The name does not say what the button does, for example a file name, address, generic word or symbols, which fails WCAG 1.1.1 (H36, F30).
The name states the button's action, such as "Submit order" or "Search".
Find the image button the report names and read the name it gives; check each listed source (alt, aria-label, aria-labelledby, title).
Press the button or read the form to learn what it does.
Decide whether the announced name says what the button does, and that the other sources do not contradict it.
invalidFieldErrorMessage_review_ERROR_ME: The error is visible but hidden from assistive technology, so screen reader users are not told what is wrong, which fails WCAG 3.3.1.
A screen reader user is told the same error text that is shown on screen, for example through the field's description or label.
Find the field the report names and confirm its error message is visible on screen.
Inspect the message element that aria-errormessage points to and note which of its children carry aria-hidden="true".
Focus the field with a screen reader running, or read its error message and description in the Accessibility pane.
Note whether the error's words reach the screen reader through any route.
No text tells the user which field is in error or what is wrong, which fails WCAG 3.3.1.
Text on the page, such as the label or a message next to the field, says which field is in error and what is wrong.
Find the field the report names and trigger its error state (submit the form or enter an invalid value) if it is not already shown.
Inspect the field and find the element its aria-errormessage attribute points to; confirm it is empty.
Look at the field's label and the text next to it for words that say which field is in error and what is wrong.
Focus the field with a screen reader running, or check its name and description in the Accessibility pane, and note whether the error is conveyed.
No text tells you which field is wrong and why, or a screen reader user isn't told, which fails WCAG 3.3.1.
The error is shown in text, and announced, somewhere tied to the field, even if not in the message aria-errormessage names.
Make the field invalid the way a user would (submit the form empty, or type a wrong value).
Look for the error message the field points to (its aria-errormessage), and check whether it appears on screen.
If it doesn't, look for any text that tells you what is wrong: in the label, next to the field, or in a summary at the top of the form.
With a screen reader, move to the field and listen for the error.
The description is only hint text and no visible text describes the error, which fails WCAG 3.3.1.
The field's description, or other visible text, states the error in words, so both sighted and screen reader users learn what is wrong.
Find the field the report names and trigger its error state if it is not already shown.
Open the Accessibility pane for the field and read its description (from aria-describedby).
Compare that description with the error: decide whether it says what is wrong, or is only hint text such as an input format.
Check that the same error text is visible on screen near the field.
The field is marked invalid but no text describes the error, which fails WCAG 3.3.1.
Once the field is in error, a shown message with that id, or other visible text, describes the error.
Find the field the report names and note the id in its aria-errormessage attribute.
Trigger the error (submit the form or enter an invalid value) and search the Elements panel for an element with that id.
If the element appears, check that it is shown and has text that describes the error.
If it never appears, look for other visible text near the field or in its label that says what is wrong.
invalidFieldErrorMessage_review_NO_ERROR: The field is in error but no text identifies it and describes the problem, which fails WCAG 3.3.1.
Visible text identifies the field in error and describes what is wrong, or the field is not actually in error.
Find the field the report names; it is marked aria-invalid.
Check whether the field is really in error now; if it is marked invalid before the user has entered anything, enter a valid value and see whether the mark clears.
Look at the field's label and the text next to it, and any error summary on the page, for words naming this field and saying what is wrong.
Focus the field with a screen reader running and note whether the error is announced.
labelForValid_review_LABEL_FOR_NOT_LABEL: The label points at an element that cannot be labelled, so the control it was meant for gets no name or focus from it, a best-practice miss under HTML's labelled-control rules.
The label is fixed to point at the control it describes, or that control already has the same name another way and the label is only visible text.
Find the label the report names and the element its for attribute points to (the report gives its tag).
Work out which form control the label was meant for.
Read that control's computed name in the Accessibility pane, and click the label to see whether it focuses the control.
labelForValid_review_LABEL_FOR_TARGET_MI: No element has that id, so the label labels nothing and its control is left without that name, a best-practice miss under HTML's labelled-control rules.
The id exists once the page is ready and the label names and focuses its control.
Find the label the report names and the id in its for attribute.
Search the page's elements for that id; check whether the control appears later, for example after a script runs.
Work out which control the label was meant for, read its computed name in the Accessibility pane, and click the label to see whether it focuses that control.
labelInName_review_HYPHENATION_DIFFERS_f: The hyphenation changes the words, so the name does not contain what the label shows, which fails WCAG 2.5.3.
labelInName_review_HYPHENATION_DIFFERS_p: The name says the same words as the label, with only the hyphenation differing, so speaking the label reaches the control.
labelInName_review_HYPHENATION_DIFFERS_s: Read the visible label of the control the report names.
Open the Accessibility pane and read the control's accessible name.
Compare the two: they differ only in where hyphens fall ("e-mail" against "email"); decide whether a person saying the visible label would say the same words.
If speech input software is available, say the visible label and see whether it activates the control.
labelInName_review_POSSIBLE_ABBREVIATION: The label's word is not read as the word in the name, so a person saying the label would not match the name, which fails WCAG 2.5.3.
The abbreviation is a conventional one read as the full word that the name contains.
Read the visible label of the control the report names, and note the word ending in a period.
Open the Accessibility pane and read the control's accessible name.
Decide whether the label's word is a common abbreviation of the word in the name ("Ave." for "Avenue") that a person would read aloud as the full word.
labelInName_review_POSSIBLE_ICON_FONT_GL: The control shows readable words that the accessible name does not contain, which fails WCAG 2.5.3.
The control shows an icon rather than readable text, or the readable text it shows is contained in the name.
Look at the control the report names on screen and note what it shows: readable words or an icon.
Open the Accessibility pane and read the control's accessible name.
If the control shows only an icon, decide whether the name describes it; if it shows readable words, check that the name contains them.
labelInName_review_POSSIBLE_SYMBOLIC_CHA: The character is text a user would say (a digit or a letter) and the name does not contain it, which fails WCAG 2.5.3.
The character is a symbol, and the name describes what it does.
Look at the single character the control the report names shows.
Open the Accessibility pane and read the control's accessible name.
Decide whether the character is a symbol standing for an action (an "X" for close, an arrow) or literal text a user would say, such as a digit or letter.
landmarkBannerIsTopLevel_review_LANDMARK: A banner sits inside another landmark, which confuses landmark navigation, a best-practice miss under the WAI-ARIA banner role.
The banner sits at the top level of the page, outside any other landmark.
Find the banner (a header or role="banner") the report names and the landmark it sits inside.
Open a screen reader's landmarks list, or the Accessibility pane, and look at where the banner appears.
Decide whether this is the page-wide header; if it is the header of an article or section, it should not be a banner.
landmarkComplementaryIsTopLevel_review_L: The complementary landmark is nested in an unrelated landmark such as a footer or navigation, which confuses landmark navigation, a best-practice miss under the WAI-ARIA complementary role.
The complementary landmark sits at the top level, or is a named related-content box inside main.
Find the complementary landmark (an aside or role="complementary") the report names and the landmark it sits inside.
Open a screen reader's landmarks list, or the Accessibility pane, and look at where it appears.
If it sits inside main and has a name, it is the common related-content box; if it sits inside a header, footer, navigation, form or another complementary, note the odd placement.
landmarkContentinfoIsTopLevel_review_LAN: A contentinfo sits inside another landmark, which confuses landmark navigation, a best-practice miss under the WAI-ARIA contentinfo role.
The contentinfo sits at the top level of the page, outside any other landmark.
Find the contentinfo (a footer or role="contentinfo") the report names and the landmark it sits inside.
Open a screen reader's landmarks list, or the Accessibility pane, and look at where it appears.
Decide whether this is the page-wide footer; if it is the footer of an article or section, it should not be a contentinfo.
landmarkMainIsTopLevel_review_LANDMARK_M: The main landmark sits inside another landmark, which confuses landmark navigation, a best-practice miss under the WAI-ARIA main role.
The main landmark sits at the top level of the page, outside any other landmark.
Find the main landmark the report names and the landmark it sits inside.
Open a screen reader's landmarks list, or the Accessibility pane, and look at where main appears.
Check whether main is the outermost container of the page's primary content.
landmarkNoDuplicateBanner_review_LANDMAR: More than one banner is exposed, so landmark navigation offers several page headers, a best-practice miss under the WAI-ARIA banner role.
Assistive technology finds only one banner, the page-wide header.
Open a screen reader's landmarks list, or the Accessibility pane, and count the banner landmarks.
For each one the report names, decide whether it is the page-wide header or the header of a section, card or dialog.
Check that hidden or closed copies (such as a header inside a closed menu) are really hidden from assistive technology.
landmarkNoDuplicateContentinfo_review_LA: More than one contentinfo is exposed, so landmark navigation offers several page footers, a best-practice miss under the WAI-ARIA contentinfo role.
Assistive technology finds only one contentinfo, the page-wide footer.
Open a screen reader's landmarks list, or the Accessibility pane, and count the contentinfo landmarks.
For each one the report names, decide whether it is the page-wide footer or the footer of a section, card or dialog.
Check that hidden or closed copies are really hidden from assistive technology.
landmarkNoDuplicateMain_review_LANDMARK_: More than one main is exposed, so users cannot tell which is the primary content, a best-practice miss under the WAI-ARIA main role and HTML's rule of one visible main.
Assistive technology finds only one main landmark, around the page's primary content.
Open a screen reader's landmarks list, or the Accessibility pane, and count the main landmarks.
For each one the report names, decide which holds the page's primary content.
Check that any other main is hidden (the hidden attribute) when it is not the current view.
landmarkOneMain_review_LANDMARK_MAIN_MIS: No main landmark is exposed, so users cannot jump straight to the primary content, a best-practice miss under the WAI-ARIA main role (ARIA11).
A main landmark exists and wraps the page's primary content.
Open a screen reader's landmarks list, or the Accessibility pane, and look for a main landmark.
Find the page's primary content and inspect its container for a main element or role="main".
If the content is inside an iframe, check the framed document for a main instead.
landmarkRoleNamePresent_review_LANDMARK_: An area meant as a landmark has no name, so it is not exposed as one, which fails the WAI-ARIA requirement that region and form roles be labelled (best practice, ARIA13).
The area does not need to be a landmark (and the role can be removed), or it is given a name that makes it one.
Inspect the element the report names and note its role (region or form).
Look at the content it wraps and any visible heading at its start.
Decide whether the area is important enough that users should be able to jump to it as a landmark.
If so, check whether it is given a name, for example with aria-labelledby pointing at its heading.
landmarkUnique_review_LANDMARK_NOT_UNIQU: Landmarks with different content share a name or have none, so they cannot be told apart when navigating by landmark (best practice, ARIA13).
The landmarks hold the same content for the same purpose (such as pagination repeated above and below a list), or each now has a distinct name that says what it is.
Find the landmarks the report names; they share one role, such as navigation, and one name or no name.
Look at each one on the page and compare what it contains and what it is for.
If they differ in purpose (for example main menu and footer links), check whether each has an aria-label or aria-labelledby that tells them apart.
Open the Accessibility pane in the browser's developer tools and confirm the name each landmark exposes.
linkInTextBlock_review_ANCESTOR_OPACITY_: The link has no non-color cue and it is told apart from the text by color alone, at less than 3:1 or with no non-color cue on hover and focus, which fails WCAG 1.4.1 (F73).
The link has a non-color cue such as an underline, bold or a border, or its color contrasts with the text by at least 3:1 and hover and focus add a non-color cue.
Find the link the report names inside its paragraph and look at it next to the surrounding text.
Check whether the link is set apart by an underline, bold, italics, a border or another mark; read colors from the screen, since the fading changes them.
If nothing but color differs, use the color picker's eyedropper in the developer tools to read the link color and the text color as drawn, and check their contrast is at least 3:1.
Then hover the pointer over the link and Tab to it, and check that an underline or another non-color mark appears.

Close any banner, dialog or overlay that is open on the page, so the page can scroll.

In the developer tools' Styles pane, add a new style rule for * setting line-height: 1.5 !important; letter-spacing: 0.12em !important; word-spacing: 0.16em !important, and a rule for p setting margin-bottom: 2em !important.
Scroll to the text the report names and check that it can be reached and read.
textboxNamePresent_review_name_internals: The text box has no name in the accessibility tree and the screen reader announces only its role, which fails WCAG 4.1.2.
The accessibility tree shows a name for the text box, set through its internals or otherwise, and the screen reader announces it.
Inspect the text box the report names, a custom element, and note its role.
Open the Accessibility pane in the browser's developer tools and read the element's accessible name.
With a screen reader, move to the element and listen to the name announced.
tooltipNamePresent_review_name_closedCon: The tooltip has no name in the accessibility tree, since its content gives none, which fails WCAG 4.1.2.
The accessibility tree shows a name for the tooltip, taken from its content, and the screen reader announces it.
Find the tooltip the report names and note the text or icon it shows on screen.
Open the Accessibility pane in the browser's developer tools and read the element's accessible name, which the browser works out from content no script can read.
With a screen reader, move to the element and listen to the name announced.
tooltipNamePresent_review_name_contentTo: The tooltip has no name in the accessibility tree, since its content gives none, which fails WCAG 4.1.2.
The accessibility tree shows a name for the tooltip, taken from its nested content, and the screen reader announces it.
Find the tooltip the report names and note the text it shows on screen.
Open the Accessibility pane in the browser's developer tools and read the element's accessible name, which the browser works out from all of its nested content.
With a screen reader, move to the element and listen to the name announced.
tooltipNamePresent_review_name_internals: The tooltip has no name in the accessibility tree and the screen reader announces only its role, which fails WCAG 4.1.2.
The accessibility tree shows a name for the tooltip, set through its internals or otherwise, and the screen reader announces it.
Inspect the tooltip the report names, a custom element, and note its role.
Open the Accessibility pane in the browser's developer tools and read the element's accessible name.
With a screen reader, move to the element and listen to the name announced.
treeitemNamePresent_review_name_closedCo: The tree item has no name in the accessibility tree, since its content gives none, which fails WCAG 4.1.2.
The accessibility tree shows a name for the tree item, taken from its content, and the screen reader announces it.
Find the tree item the report names and note the text or icon it shows on screen.
Open the Accessibility pane in the browser's developer tools and read the element's accessible name, which the browser works out from content no script can read.
With a screen reader, move to the element and listen to the name announced.
treeitemNamePresent_review_name_contentT: The tree item has no name in the accessibility tree, since its content gives none, which fails WCAG 4.1.2.
The accessibility tree shows a name for the tree item, taken from its nested content, and the screen reader announces it.
Find the tree item the report names and note the text it shows on screen.
Open the Accessibility pane in the browser's developer tools and read the element's accessible name, which the browser works out from all of its nested content.
With a screen reader, move to the element and listen to the name announced.
treeitemNamePresent_review_name_internal: The tree item has no name in the accessibility tree and the screen reader announces only its role, which fails WCAG 4.1.2.
The accessibility tree shows a name for the tree item, set through its internals or otherwise, and the screen reader announces it.
Inspect the tree item the report names, a custom element, and note its role.
Open the Accessibility pane in the browser's developer tools and read the element's accessible name.
With a screen reader, move to the element and listen to the name announced.
videoCaption_review_CAPTIONS_REVIEW_fail: Captions are missing parts of the dialogue or important sounds, or are out of sync, which fails WCAG 1.2.2 (F8).
videoCaption_review_CAPTIONS_REVIEW_pass: The captions carry all dialogue and the important sounds, in time with the video.
videoCaption_review_CAPTIONS_REVIEW_step: Play the video the report names and turn on its captions.
Watch with the sound on and compare the captions with what is said and heard.
Check they carry all dialogue, say who is speaking when it is not clear, and describe sounds that matter (music, alarms, laughter), and that they stay in time.
videoCaption_review_CAPTIONS_TRACK_NOT_D: The video has dialogue or important sounds and no captions, here or in a linked captioned version, even if a transcript is offered, which fails WCAG 1.2.2.
The video has no meaningful audio, captions (in this video or in a captioned version linked next to it) cover the dialogue and sounds, or it is a labelled media alternative for text on the page.
Play the video the report names with the sound on and note whether it has speech or sounds that carry information.
If it is silent or only background music with no meaning, it needs no captions.

Otherwise look for captions: the player's CC button, captions burned into the picture, or a link next to the video to a captioned version of the same video. A transcript on its own does not replace captions.
videoCaption_review_SUBTITLES_TRACK_ONLY: The track gives the words only, with no speaker or sound information that matters, which fails WCAG 1.2.2.
The track carries the dialogue plus the speaker and sound information, so it works as captions, or the video has no audio that needs captions.
Play the video the report names and turn on its subtitle track.
Watch with the sound on and compare the text with what is heard.
Check that besides the dialogue it says who is speaking when it is not clear and describes sounds that matter.
videoPoster_textAltPresent_review_VIDEO_: The caption does not identify the video, so the poster has no text alternative, which fails WCAG 1.1.1.
The caption identifies the video and what its poster shows.
Find the video the report names and look at its poster image before it plays.
Read the figure's caption shown with it.
Decide whether the caption tells someone who cannot see the poster what the video is.
widgetKeyboardFocusable_review_ACTIVEDES: The element cannot get focus, so moving through items announces nothing or the items cannot be reached, and the choices cannot be made another way with the keyboard, which fails WCAG 2.1.1.

The element gets focus and the screen reader announces each active item as the arrow keys move, or the same choices can be made another way with the keyboard alone and the screen reader announces them.
Find the element the report names; it uses aria-activedescendant to point at its active item.
Using only the keyboard, open or reach the widget (for example type in its search box) and watch whether that element, not something else, gets focus.
Press the arrow keys with a screen reader running and listen whether each active item is announced.

If the items cannot be reached this way, check whether the same choices can be made another way with the keyboard alone, for example by typing the value into a text field. It only counts if every choice is available that way and a screen reader announces it.
widgetKeyboardFocusable_review_COMPOSITE: Focus never gets into the widget or its items with the keyboard, and what they do cannot be done another way with the keyboard, which fails WCAG 2.1.1.
Tab (or the button that opens it) puts focus in the widget and the arrow keys move between its items, or everything its items do can be done another way with the keyboard alone.
Find the widget the report names (a menu, list box, tab list, toolbar, grid or tree).
Click just before it and press Tab, and watch whether focus enters it or one of its items.
If it is a popup, open it from its button with the keyboard and see whether focus moves into it.
Once inside, check that the arrow keys move between the items.

If focus never gets in, check whether what the widget does can be done another way with the keyboard alone, for example the same choices offered as links or buttons elsewhere on the page. It only counts if every option the widget offers is available that way.
widgetKeyboardFocusable_review_WIDGET_NO: The widget cannot be reached or used with the keyboard and its function is not offered elsewhere, which fails WCAG 2.1.1 (F42).
The widget gets keyboard focus and works with the keyboard, or the same function is offered by another keyboard-reachable control.
Find the widget the report names and note what it does when clicked or touched.
Click just before it, then press Tab and watch whether focus ever lands on it.
If it never gets focus, look for another control a keyboard can reach that does the same thing.
If the element does nothing, its role may be wrong; note that instead.
Tab and arrow keys never reach the widget and nothing else offers its function, which fails WCAG 2.1.1.
Focus is moved to the widget by script or by arrow keys when needed, or its function is offered elsewhere.
Find the widget the report names and note when it appears (for example when a menu or dialog opens).
Use only the keyboard to open or reach that part of the page, and watch whether a script moves focus to the widget, or the arrow keys reach it.
If focus never reaches it, look for another keyboard-reachable control that does the same thing.
wcag_1.4.12_avoid-inline-spacing_step1: In the developer tools' Elements pane, search the page's markup (Ctrl+F, or Cmd+F on a Mac) for !important, and note each match in a style attribute that sets line-height, letter-spacing or word-spacing.
wcag_1.4.12_avoid-inline-spacing_step2: For each, read the resulting value in the Computed tab and compare it with 1.5 times the font size for line-height, 0.12 times for letter-spacing and 0.16 times for word-spacing.
wcag_1.4.12_avoid-inline-spacing_step3: Where the value is lower, narrow the window to 320 CSS pixels wide and check whether that text wraps onto more than one line.
wcag_1.4.12_avoid-inline-spacing_step4: In the developer tools' Styles pane, add a new style rule for * setting line-height: 1.5 !important; letter-spacing: 0.12em !important; word-spacing: 0.16em !important, and a rule for p setting margin-bottom: 2em !important. The element keeps its own value, since its style attribute wins.
wcag_1.4.12_avoid-inline-spacing_step5: Check whether that text is cut off, overlaps other text or is hidden.
wcag_1.4.12_avoid-inline-spacing_pass: No style attribute forces spacing below those values on text that wraps, or the text it forces still shows in full with the spacing applied.
wcag_1.4.12_avoid-inline-spacing_fail: A style attribute forces spacing below those values on wrapping text, so a person can't apply their own, and lines overlap or text is cut off, which fails WCAG 1.4.12.
wcag_1.4.12_text-spacing-content-loss_st: In the developer tools' Styles pane, add a new style rule for * setting line-height: 1.5 !important; letter-spacing: 0.12em !important; word-spacing: 0.16em !important, and a rule for p setting margin-bottom: 2em !important. Rules added in the Styles pane are not blocked by the page's security policy.
Scroll through the whole page and look for text that is cut off, overlaps other text or disappears. Text that is part of an image doesn't count.

Where text is cut off, check whether the page offers a way to show all of it, such as a "Read more" link or a button that expands the box. It only counts if you can use it with the keyboard and, with the spacing still applied, it shows the whole text.
wcag_1.4.12_text-spacing-content-loss_pa: All text stays visible and readable, or any text that is cut off can be shown in full with the keyboard.
wcag_1.4.12_text-spacing-content-loss_fa: Some text is cut off, overlaps or is lost with the spacing applied and cannot be shown in full another way, which fails WCAG 1.4.12.
wcag_1.4.12_text-spacing-functionality-k: In the developer tools' Styles pane, add a new style rule for * setting line-height: 1.5 !important; letter-spacing: 0.12em !important; word-spacing: 0.16em !important, and a rule for p setting margin-bottom: 2em !important.
Use each control on the page: open its menus and drop-downs, fill in and submit its forms, switch its tabs, and open and close its dialogs.
Check that each still responds, that no text pushed out of place covers a control, and that every label and button shows all its text.
Every control still works and shows all its text with the spacing applied.
With the spacing applied, a control stops working, is covered so it can't be used, or loses text that says what it does, which fails WCAG 1.4.12.
wcag_1.4.12_text-spacing-other-states_st: In the developer tools' Styles pane, add a new style rule for * setting line-height: 1.5 !important; letter-spacing: 0.12em !important; word-spacing: 0.16em !important, and a rule for p setting margin-bottom: 2em !important.

Bring up the content the page shows only after you do something: open each menu and dialog, switch to each tab, expand each collapsed section, show each tooltip, and submit a form with a mistake in it to see its error messages.
Check each for text that is cut off, overlaps other text or disappears, as on the page itself.

Where text is cut off, check whether the page offers a way to show all of it, such as a "Read more" link or a button that expands the box. It only counts if you can use it with the keyboard and, with the spacing still applied, it shows the whole text.
wcag_1.4.12_text-spacing-other-states_pa: Content shown after you do something keeps all its text visible and readable with the spacing applied, or the text that is cut off can be shown in full with the keyboard.
wcag_1.4.12_text-spacing-other-states_fa: Text in a menu, dialog, tab, tooltip or message is cut off or overlaps with the spacing applied and can't be shown in full another way, which fails WCAG 1.4.12.
wcag_1.4.13_hover-focus-content-dismissi: Move the pointer slowly over the page, over icons, links, buttons, abbreviations and form fields, and note every tooltip, popup or submenu that appears. Leave out the small tooltip the browser draws for a title attribute: it is exempt.
Click the address bar, then press Tab through the page and note any such content that appears when an element receives focus.
Show each one again, by hovering or by focus, and without moving the pointer or focus, press Escape.
