Where Escape doesn't close it, check whether it covers or pushes aside any other content, and whether it only reports an input error, such as a message beside a field.
Each piece of extra content closes with Escape (or another key the page tells you about) without the pointer or focus moving, or covers and pushes aside nothing, or only reports an input error.
Extra content covers or pushes aside other content and closes only when the pointer or focus moves, so someone who magnifies the screen can't see what it hides, which fails WCAG 1.4.13.
wcag_1.4.13_hover-content-hoverable_step: Move the pointer over the page and note each element that shows extra content when the pointer is over it, such as a tooltip or a submenu. Leave out the small tooltip the browser draws for a title attribute: it is exempt.
Show each one again, then move the pointer slowly from the element onto the extra content and over all of it.
Where the content is too long to see at once, scroll it or move over the part that is cut off.
wcag_1.4.13_hover-content-hoverable_pass: The extra content stays while the pointer moves from the element onto it and over all of it.
wcag_1.4.13_hover-content-hoverable_fail: The extra content disappears as the pointer moves onto it, so someone who magnifies the screen, and must move the pointer to read it, can't, which fails WCAG 1.4.13.
wcag_1.4.13_hover-focus-content-persiste: Show each piece of extra content the page has, once by hovering and, where it also appears on focus, once by pressing Tab to its element.
Keep the pointer and focus where they are and press nothing for at least 30 seconds, watching the content.
Where the content goes away by itself, check whether what it said is no longer true, such as "Saving…" once the saving has finished.
The content stays until you move the pointer or focus away or close it, or goes away only once what it says is no longer true.
The content disappears on a timer while the pointer or focus is still on its element, before you close it, which fails WCAG 1.4.13.
wcag_2.4.3_focus-order-preserves-meaning: Click the address bar, then press Tab repeatedly until focus has been through the whole page, watching where it goes.
Compare the order with the order in which you would read and use the page: a form's fields in the order of their labels, for example, and the steps of a task in their sequence.
Press Shift+Tab back through the page and check that focus goes back the same way in reverse.
Where the order differs from the reading order, check whether that changes what something means or keeps you from using it, such as reaching a form's Submit button before its fields.
Focus moves through the page in an order that keeps its meaning and lets every part be used, even where it differs from the visual order in small ways.
Focus jumps around the page so that its meaning or use changes, such as fields filled in out of their order, which fails WCAG 2.4.3.
wcag_2.4.3_focus-order-opened-content_st: With the keyboard, open each dialog, menu, drop-down and collapsed section the page has, by pressing Enter or Space on the control that opens it.
Press Tab once and check that focus goes into what opened, or is already in it, rather than to something behind it or far from it.
In a dialog that covers the page, press Tab until you have been through all its controls, and check that focus stays in the dialog rather than going to the page behind it.
Close it with Escape or its close button, and check that focus goes back to the control that opened it, or to the next sensible place.
wcag_2.4.3_focus-order-opened-content_pa: Focus goes into what opens, stays in a dialog while it covers the page, and comes back to where it was when it closes.
wcag_2.4.3_focus-order-opened-content_fa: Focus stays behind what opens, leaves a dialog for the page behind it, or lands at the top of the page when it closes, so the order no longer follows what is on screen, which fails WCAG 2.4.3.
wcag_2.4.3_focus-order-no-hidden-stops_s: Close any menu or dialog, click the address bar, then press Tab through the whole page, watching where focus is.
Note each time focus seems to disappear for one or more presses.
At each such stop, type document.activeElement in the developer tools' Console and check whether the element it shows is in a closed menu, a hidden panel or off screen.
Leave out a skip link that appears when it receives focus: it is shown once focused.
wcag_2.4.3_focus-order-no-hidden-stops_p: Every Tab stop is on something you can see, or on something that appears when it receives focus, such as a skip link.
wcag_2.4.3_focus-order-no-hidden-stops_f: Focus stops on controls in closed menus, hidden panels or off screen, so the order passes through things that aren't there, which fails WCAG 2.4.3.
wcag_1.1.1_text-alternative-mechanism_st: Look through the whole page for content that isn't text: photos, icons, logos, charts, maps, diagrams, video posters, and the pictures inside buttons and links.
For each, select it in the developer tools' Elements pane and read the Name in its Accessibility pane.
Note each one that has no name and isn't hidden from assistive technology (with alt="", aria-hidden="true", role="presentation" or as a CSS background).
For content that can't be described in a few words, such as a chart or a map, check that the name at least says what it is, and that a fuller description is on the page or linked beside it.
wcag_1.1.1_text-alternative-mechanism_pa: Every piece of non-text content a person needs has a text alternative, or is hidden from assistive technology because it is decorative.
wcag_1.1.1_text-alternative-mechanism_fa: Non-text content that conveys something has no text alternative, so a screen reader user meets an unnamed image or nothing at all, which fails WCAG 1.1.1.
wcag_1.1.1_functional-nontext-name_step1: Find every link, button and other control whose only content is an image or icon, such as a logo that links home, a magnifier for search or a cross that closes a dialog.
wcag_1.1.1_functional-nontext-name_step2: For each, select it in the developer tools' Elements pane and read the Name in its Accessibility pane.
wcag_1.1.1_functional-nontext-name_step3: Check that the name says what the control does or where it leads ("Search", "Close", "Home"), not what the picture shows ("magnifying glass") or a file name.
wcag_1.1.1_functional-nontext-name_pass: Every control made of an image or icon has a name that says what it does or where it goes.
wcag_1.1.1_functional-nontext-name_fail: A control made of an image or icon has no name, or one that describes the picture rather than what it does, which fails WCAG 1.1.1.
wcag_1.1.1_decorative-null_step1: Look through the page for images, icons and graphics that only decorate: borders, dividers, background pictures, ornaments, and pictures whose content the text next to them already gives.
wcag_1.1.1_decorative-null_step2: For each, select it in the developer tools' Elements pane and check in its Accessibility pane that it is ignored (alt="", aria-hidden="true", role="presentation", or a CSS background).
wcag_1.1.1_decorative-null_step3: Then do the reverse: for each image that is hidden that way, ask whether a user would miss anything if it were gone: information, a label, a chart's data.
wcag_1.1.1_decorative-null_pass: Decorative images are hidden from assistive technology, and every image that is hidden is truly decorative.
wcag_1.1.1_decorative-null_fail: A decorative image is announced (often by its file name), or an image that conveys information is hidden from assistive technology, which fails WCAG 1.1.1.
wcag_1.1.1_text-alternative-quality_step: For each image and other non-text content that has a text alternative, read the alternative (the Name in the developer tools' Accessibility pane) and look at the content in its place on the page.
Ask what the content gives a reader there, and check that the alternative gives the same: the words in an image of text, the point a photo makes, the facts a chart shows.

Where the alternative only names a complex image, such as a chart or diagram, check that the details are in a caption, text or table next to it, or a link beside it, that a screen reader user can find from the image.
Note alternatives that are a file name, a web address, a word such as "image" or "photo", or that repeat the text right next to them.
wcag_1.1.1_text-alternative-quality_pass: Each text alternative gives what its content gives in that place, directly or through a description a screen reader user can reach from it.
wcag_1.1.1_text-alternative-quality_fail: A text alternative doesn't give what the content does, for example a file name, a generic word or a chart named without its data anywhere, which fails WCAG 1.1.1 (F30).
wcag_1.1.1_captcha-alternative_step1: Find any test the page uses to tell people from programs, such as distorted letters to type, pictures to pick or a puzzle to drag.
wcag_1.1.1_captcha-alternative_step2: Check that it has a text alternative that says what it is and what to do, without giving the answer away.
wcag_1.1.1_captcha-alternative_step3: Check that it offers another form that uses a different sense, such as an audio version of a visual test, or another way altogether, such as a code by email.
wcag_1.1.1_captcha-alternative_step4: Try the other form with a screen reader and the keyboard.
wcag_1.1.1_captcha-alternative_pass: The page has no such test, or the test says what it is and offers a form that uses another sense and can be completed.
wcag_1.1.1_captcha-alternative_fail: The test can only be passed by seeing (or only by hearing), or has no text saying what it is, which fails WCAG 1.1.1.
wcag_1.2.1_transcript-evidence_step1: Find every audio player and every video without sound on the page, including ones in frames, and play each.
wcag_1.2.1_transcript-evidence_step2: For audio, look next to the player and elsewhere on the page for a transcript or a link to one.
wcag_1.2.1_transcript-evidence_step3: For a video without sound, look for a transcript, or an audio version that describes everything shown, that you can find and play from the page with the keyboard.
wcag_1.2.1_transcript-evidence_step4: Compare each alternative with the media and check that it gives the same information: speech, important sounds and what is shown.
wcag_1.2.1_transcript-evidence_step5: Leave out media that is itself an alternative for text on the page and is labelled as such.
wcag_1.2.1_transcript-evidence_pass: Every prerecorded audio-only or video-only item has a transcript, or for video an audio version, that gives what it gives, or is a labelled alternative for text on the page.
wcag_1.2.1_transcript-evidence_fail: Prerecorded audio-only media has no transcript, or prerecorded video-only media has neither a transcript nor an audio version with the same information, which fails WCAG 1.2.1.
wcag_1.2.2_video-captions-track-evidence: Find every prerecorded video with sound on the page, including ones in frames and players of other sites.
Play each with the sound on and note whether its sound carries information: speech, or sounds that matter.

Where it does, look for captions: the player's CC button, captions burned into the picture, or a captioned version of the same video linked next to it. A transcript on its own doesn't replace captions.
Leave out a video that is itself an alternative for text on the page and is labelled as such.
Every prerecorded video whose sound carries information has captions, here or in a captioned version linked next to it, or is a labelled alternative for text on the page.
A prerecorded video has dialogue or important sounds and no captions, here or in a linked captioned version, even if a transcript is offered, which fails WCAG 1.2.2.
wcag_1.2.2_captions-complete_step1: Play each captioned video with the sound on and the captions turned on.
wcag_1.2.2_captions-complete_step2: Compare the captions with what is said and heard, all the way through.
wcag_1.2.2_captions-complete_step3: Check that they carry all the dialogue, say who is speaking when that isn't clear, and describe the sounds that matter (music, alarms, laughter), and that they stay in time with the picture.
wcag_1.2.2_captions-complete_pass: The captions carry all dialogue, the speakers where needed, and the important sounds, in time with the video.
wcag_1.2.2_captions-complete_fail: Captions leave out dialogue or important sounds, don't say who is speaking where that matters, or run out of time with the video, which fails WCAG 1.2.2 (F8).
wcag_1.2.3_audio-description-or-alternat: Find every prerecorded video with sound on the page and play each with the sound on.
Note what the picture shows that the sound doesn't say: actions, scene changes, text on screen, who is there.
Look for an audio description (a version, or a track the player offers, where a voice says what is shown) or a text alternative next to the video that tells the whole story, sound and picture.
Where there is one, check that it covers what you noted.
Leave out a video that is itself an alternative for text on the page and is labelled as such, and one whose picture adds nothing the sound doesn't say.
Each video whose picture shows something the sound doesn't say has an audio description or a full text alternative that gives it.
A prerecorded video shows information the sound doesn't give, with neither an audio description nor a full text alternative, which fails WCAG 1.2.3.
wcag_1.2.4_live-captions_step1: Find any live video with sound on the page: a stream, a webcast, a live event.
wcag_1.2.4_live-captions_step2: While it is live, turn on its captions in the player, or look for captions shown with it on the page.
wcag_1.2.4_live-captions_step3: Watch for a few minutes with the sound on and check that the captions follow the speech and the sounds that matter, with only the short delay live captions need.
wcag_1.2.4_live-captions_pass: The page has no live video with sound, or its live video has captions that follow what is said.
wcag_1.2.4_live-captions_fail: Live video with sound has no captions, or captions that leave out most of what is said, which fails WCAG 1.2.4.
wcag_1.2.5_audio-description_step1: Find every prerecorded video with sound on the page and play each with the sound on.
wcag_1.2.5_audio-description_step2: Note what the picture shows that the sound doesn't say: actions, scene changes, text on screen, who is there.
wcag_1.2.5_audio-description_step3: Look for an audio description: a track the player offers (an AD or description button, or an audio-language choice), or a described version of the video linked next to it.
wcag_1.2.5_audio-description_step4: Play it and check that a voice says what you noted, in the pauses of the speech.
wcag_1.2.5_audio-description_step5: Leave out a video whose picture adds nothing the sound doesn't say: it needs no description.
wcag_1.2.5_audio-description_pass: Each video whose picture shows something the sound doesn't say has an audio description that gives it.
wcag_1.2.5_audio-description_fail: A prerecorded video shows information the sound doesn't give and has no audio description; a text alternative alone isn't enough at this level, which fails WCAG 1.2.5.
wcag_1.3.1_headings-marked-up_step1: Look through the page and note every piece of text that works as a heading: it is larger or bolder than the text around it and introduces what follows.
wcag_1.3.1_headings-marked-up_step2: For each, check in the developer tools' Elements pane that it is an <h1> to <h6>, or has role="heading" with an aria-level.
wcag_1.3.1_headings-marked-up_step3: Check the reverse: each heading element on the page introduces content, rather than being used only to make text big.
wcag_1.3.1_headings-marked-up_step4: List the headings with a screen reader's headings list, or in the Accessibility pane, and check that their levels follow the page's outline: a section's sub-headings one level below its heading.
wcag_1.3.1_headings-marked-up_pass: Every visual heading is marked up as a heading, every heading element is one, and the levels follow the outline the page shows.
wcag_1.3.1_headings-marked-up_fail: Text that looks like a heading is plain text, a heading element is used only for its size, or the levels contradict the outline, so screen reader users can't find or follow the sections, which fails WCAG 1.3.1.
wcag_1.3.1_lists-marked-up_step1: Look through the page for content shown as a list: items in a row or column with bullets, numbers or the same layout, such as menus, steps and groups of links.
wcag_1.3.1_lists-marked-up_step2: For each, check in the developer tools' Elements pane that it is a <ul>, <ol> or <dl> (or has role="list" with role="listitem" items).
wcag_1.3.1_lists-marked-up_step3: Check that each list holds only list items directly, and each list item sits in a list.
wcag_1.3.1_lists-marked-up_pass: Content shown as a list is marked up as a list, and list markup is complete.
wcag_1.3.1_lists-marked-up_fail: Content shown as a list is a run of paragraphs, line breaks or divs, or list markup is broken, so a screen reader doesn't say it is a list or how many items it has, which fails WCAG 1.3.1.
wcag_1.3.1_tables-marked-up_step1: Find every table on the page, and every grid of data drawn without a table.
wcag_1.3.1_tables-marked-up_step2: For a table of data, check in the developer tools' Elements pane that its header cells are <th> (with scope where a header is not plainly a row or column header) and that a title shown above it is its <caption>.
wcag_1.3.1_tables-marked-up_step3: For a complex table, with headers on more than one level, check that each data cell names its headers with a headers attribute or scope.
wcag_1.3.1_tables-marked-up_step4: With a screen reader, move through a few data cells and check that it reads their headers with them.
wcag_1.3.1_tables-marked-up_step5: For a table used only to lay things out, check that it has no <th>, <caption> or summary.
wcag_1.3.1_tables-marked-up_pass: Data is in tables whose headers and caption are marked up, a screen reader reads each cell's headers, and layout tables carry no header markup.
wcag_1.3.1_tables-marked-up_fail: A table of data has no header markup or a fake caption in a cell, data is laid out as a grid without a table, or a layout table is marked up as data, which fails WCAG 1.3.1.
wcag_1.3.1_form-labels-associated_step1: Find every form field on the page: text fields, check boxes, radio buttons, drop-downs and custom controls.
wcag_1.3.1_form-labels-associated_step2: For each, select it in the developer tools' Elements pane and check that the Name in its Accessibility pane contains its visible label.
wcag_1.3.1_form-labels-associated_step3: For a group of fields under one question, such as radio buttons or a date in three parts, check that the group is a <fieldset> with a <legend>, or has role="group" with a name, so the question is read with each field.
wcag_1.3.1_form-labels-associated_step4: Check that instructions shown next to a field (a format, a required mark) are tied to it with aria-describedby or are in its label.
wcag_1.3.1_form-labels-associated_pass: Every field's name includes its visible label, groups of fields are named by their question, and a field's instructions are tied to it.
wcag_1.3.1_form-labels-associated_fail: A field is labelled only by nearby text that isn't tied to it, or a group's question isn't tied to its fields, so a screen reader reads a field without saying what it is for, which fails WCAG 1.3.1.
wcag_1.3.1_aria-structure-valid_step1: Find the parts of the page built with ARIA roles: custom menus, tabs, trees, grids, lists and listboxes.
wcag_1.3.1_aria-structure-valid_step2: For each, open the developer tools' Accessibility tree and check that the structure it shows matches what is on screen: a tablist holding tabs, a menu holding menu items, a grid holding rows and cells.
wcag_1.3.1_aria-structure-valid_step3: Check that no element with a role is missing the parent or children its role needs, and that aria-owns, where used, gives each element a single owner.
wcag_1.3.1_aria-structure-valid_step4: Check that <body> is not hidden with aria-hidden="true".
wcag_1.3.1_aria-structure-valid_pass: The accessibility tree gives the structure the page shows, with every role in the place its role needs.
wcag_1.3.1_aria-structure-valid_fail: A role is missing its required parent or children, owned twice, or the page is hidden from the tree, so assistive technology gives a structure that doesn't match the screen, which fails WCAG 1.3.1.
wcag_1.3.1_visual-cues-conveyed_step1: Look for meaning that the page shows only by how things look: required fields marked by an asterisk or color, emphasized or struck-through words, a selected item shown by its style, text set apart in a box.
wcag_1.3.1_visual-cues-conveyed_step2: For each, check whether the same meaning is in the markup (such as required, aria-current, <em>, <del>) or in the text itself ("required", "current page").
wcag_1.3.1_visual-cues-conveyed_step3: Read the parts with a screen reader and check that what the styling shows is said.
wcag_1.3.1_visual-cues-conveyed_pass: Whatever the styling or layout conveys is also in the markup or the text.
wcag_1.3.1_visual-cues-conveyed_fail: Meaning is given only by styling or position, such as required fields marked only by color or an unexplained asterisk, so a screen reader user misses it, which fails WCAG 1.3.1.
wcag_1.3.2_reading-order-meaningful_step: Have a screen reader read the whole page from the top, or read the content in the order of the developer tools' Elements pane, and follow along on screen.
Note where the order read differs from the order you see: columns read across, a caption read far from its image, a step read before the one it follows.
Where it differs, ask whether the meaning changes: it does if the content only makes sense in the order shown.
Look for text laid out with spaces or line breaks, such as letters spaced apart in a word or columns made of spaces, and check how a screen reader reads it.
wcag_1.3.2_reading-order-meaningful_pass: Content is read in an order that keeps its meaning, and no text is laid out with spaces in a way that breaks words or columns.
wcag_1.3.2_reading-order-meaningful_fail: Content is read in an order that changes its meaning, such as a table's columns read across, or words are spaced out letter by letter, which fails WCAG 1.3.2.
wcag_1.3.3_instructions-not-sensory-only: Read every instruction on the page: form help, error messages, and text that tells you where to look or what to press.
Note each that identifies something only by how it looks, where it is or how it sounds: "the round button", "the menu on the right", "the items in green", "after the beep".
For each, check whether it also names the thing in a way that doesn't depend on seeing or hearing it, such as its label ("the Search button on the right").
Every instruction names what it refers to by its label or text, besides any shape, color, position or sound.
An instruction identifies something only by its shape, color, size, position or sound, so someone who can't see or hear it can't follow it, which fails WCAG 1.3.3.
wcag_1.3.4_orientation-not-locked_step1: Open the page in the developer tools' device toolbar, or on a phone or tablet.
wcag_1.3.4_orientation-not-locked_step2: View it in portrait, then rotate it to landscape (or the reverse), and use its main content and controls in each.
wcag_1.3.4_orientation-not-locked_step3: Check that the page doesn't ask you to rotate the device, turn its content sideways, or hide content in one orientation.
wcag_1.3.4_orientation-not-locked_step4: Where it does, ask whether that orientation is essential, as for a bank cheque or a piano keyboard.
wcag_1.3.4_orientation-not-locked_pass: The page shows and works in both orientations, or one orientation is essential to it.
wcag_1.3.4_orientation-not-locked_fail: The page works in only one orientation, by asking to rotate the device, turning its content or hiding it, with no essential reason, which fails WCAG 1.3.4.
wcag_1.3.5_input-purpose-identified_step: Find every field that asks for information about the person using the page: name, email, phone, address, birthday, username, password, card details.
For each, read its autocomplete attribute in the developer tools' Elements pane.
Check that it is the value that matches what the field asks for (name, email, tel, street-address, postal-code, bday, username, new-password, cc-number and so on).
Leave out fields that ask about someone else, such as a gift recipient, unless they say so with the right section or value.
wcag_1.3.5_input-purpose-identified_pass: Every field that asks for the user's own information has the autocomplete value that matches it.
wcag_1.3.5_input-purpose-identified_fail: A field that asks for the user's own information has no autocomplete value, or a wrong one, so the browser and assistive tools can't fill it in or mark its purpose, which fails WCAG 1.3.5.
wcag_1.4.1_color-not-only-means_step1: Look for information the page gives by color: links in a paragraph, required or invalid fields, the selected tab or day, chart series, status in red or green.
wcag_1.4.1_color-not-only-means_step2: For each, check whether something besides color gives it too: an underline, an icon, a text label, a pattern, a border or a change of shape.
wcag_1.4.1_color-not-only-means_step3: For links in a paragraph that differ only by color, check that they get an underline or other mark when hovered and focused, and that their color has a contrast of at least 3:1 with the text around them.
wcag_1.4.1_color-not-only-means_step4: View the page in grayscale (in the developer tools' Rendering pane, emulate achromatopsia) and check that nothing is lost.
wcag_1.4.1_color-not-only-means_pass: Everything the page gives by color is also given another way.
wcag_1.4.1_color-not-only-means_fail: Information, such as which fields have errors or which text is a link, is given only by color, which fails WCAG 1.4.1.
wcag_1.4.2_no-autoplay-audio-evidence_st: Load the page with the sound on and listen for sound that starts by itself: music, a video, an advertisement.
Where sound plays for more than 3 seconds, look near the top of the page or the player for a way to pause or stop it, or to turn its volume down apart from the computer's volume.
Check that the control can be found and used with the keyboard.
wcag_1.4.2_no-autoplay-audio-evidence_pa: No sound plays by itself for more than 3 seconds, or a control near the start of the page pauses, stops or lowers it.
wcag_1.4.2_no-autoplay-audio-evidence_fa: Sound plays by itself for more than 3 seconds with no way to pause, stop or lower it apart from the computer's volume, so it drowns out a screen reader, which fails WCAG 1.4.2.
wcag_1.4.3_contrast-minimum-text_step1: Look through the page for text that seems faint against its background: light gray text, text on colored panels, placeholders, text over images or gradients, text in buttons.
wcag_1.4.3_contrast-minimum-text_step2: For each, inspect it and click the swatch of its color in the developer tools' Styles pane: the picker shows its contrast ratio with the background.
wcag_1.4.3_contrast-minimum-text_step3: Where the background is an image, a gradient or a semi-transparent layer, measure the text against the part of the background where it is least visible, with a color contrast checker.
wcag_1.4.3_contrast-minimum-text_step4: Check the ratio is at least 4.5:1, or 3:1 for large text: at least 24 pixels (18pt), or 18.66 pixels (14pt) and bold.
wcag_1.4.3_contrast-minimum-text_step5: Leave out text in logos, text on disabled controls, and text that is only decoration.
wcag_1.4.3_contrast-minimum-text_pass: All text and images of text have a contrast of at least 4.5:1 with their background, or 3:1 when large.
wcag_1.4.3_contrast-minimum-text_fail: Text has less contrast with its background than 4.5:1 (3:1 for large text), so people with low vision can't read it, which fails WCAG 1.4.3.
wcag_1.4.4_text-resizes-200_step2: Go through the whole page and check that all text has grown, and none is cut off, overlapped or hidden.
wcag_1.4.4_text-resizes-200_step3: Use the page's controls, menus and forms at that size and check that they all still work.
wcag_1.4.4_text-resizes-200_step4: On a phone, or in the developer tools' device toolbar, check that you can pinch to zoom the page to 200%.
wcag_1.4.4_text-resizes-200_pass: At 200% all text has grown and stays readable, and everything still works.
wcag_1.4.4_text-resizes-200_fail: At 200% text is cut off, overlaps or doesn't grow, a control stops working, or pinch zoom is blocked, which fails WCAG 1.4.4.
wcag_1.4.5_text-not-as-image_step1: Look for images that contain words: banners, headings, buttons, quotes, menus.
wcag_1.4.5_text-not-as-image_step2: Try to select a word of it with the pointer, or inspect it: text that can't be selected is usually in an image, an SVG drawing or a canvas.
wcag_1.4.5_text-not-as-image_step3: For each, ask whether the same could be shown with real text styled with CSS.
wcag_1.4.5_text-not-as-image_step4: Leave out logos and brand names, and images where the particular look of the text is essential, such as a font sample.
wcag_1.4.5_text-not-as-image_pass: Text is real text, or an image of text is a logo or needs its exact look.
wcag_1.4.5_text-not-as-image_fail: Words are shown as an image where styled text would look the same, so people can't resize, recolor or respace them, which fails WCAG 1.4.5.
wcag_1.4.10_reflow-320_step1: In the developer tools' device toolbar, set the page to 320 CSS pixels wide (or set the window to 1280 pixels wide and zoom to 400%).
wcag_1.4.10_reflow-320_step2: Scroll down through the whole page and check that you never need to scroll sideways to read text or reach a control.
wcag_1.4.10_reflow-320_step3: Check that nothing is cut off, overlaps or is hidden, and that menus, dialogs and forms still work.
wcag_1.4.10_reflow-320_step4: Leave out content that needs two dimensions to make sense, such as maps, data tables, diagrams and toolbars: those may scroll sideways on their own.
wcag_1.4.10_reflow-320_pass: At 320 CSS pixels wide the page reads in one column with vertical scrolling only, apart from content that needs two dimensions, and nothing is lost.
wcag_1.4.10_reflow-320_fail: At 320 CSS pixels wide text must be scrolled sideways to be read, or content or controls are cut off or lost, which fails WCAG 1.4.10.
wcag_1.4.11_ui-component-contrast_step1: Find the page's controls whose outline or shape you need to see to find them: text fields, check boxes, radio buttons, toggles, buttons without a filled background, sliders.
wcag_1.4.11_ui-component-contrast_step2: Measure the color of the edge or shape that shows each one against the color next to it, with the developer tools' color picker or a color contrast checker.
wcag_1.4.11_ui-component-contrast_step3: Do the same for what shows each control's state: a check mark, the selected tab, the focus indicator as you press Tab.
wcag_1.4.11_ui-component-contrast_step4: Leave out controls the browser draws without the page's styling, and disabled controls.
wcag_1.4.11_ui-component-contrast_pass: What shows each control and its state has a contrast of at least 3:1 with what is next to it.
wcag_1.4.11_ui-component-contrast_fail: A field border, a check box, a toggle's state or a focus indicator has less than 3:1 contrast with what is next to it, so people with low vision can't find it or tell its state, which fails WCAG 1.4.11.
wcag_1.4.11_graphics-contrast_step1: Find the graphics that carry information: icons without text, charts, diagrams, maps, infographics.
wcag_1.4.11_graphics-contrast_step2: Note the parts you need to understand each one: an icon's shape, a chart's lines, bars and slices, the arrows in a diagram.
wcag_1.4.11_graphics-contrast_step3: Measure each part against the colors next to it with a color contrast checker.
wcag_1.4.11_graphics-contrast_step4: Leave out a part whose information is also given in text next to it, such as values labelled on a chart, and logos.
wcag_1.4.11_graphics-contrast_pass: Every part of a graphic needed to understand it has a contrast of at least 3:1 with what is next to it, or its information is also given as text.
wcag_1.4.11_graphics-contrast_fail: A part of a graphic needed to understand it, such as a chart's line or an icon, has less than 3:1 contrast, which fails WCAG 1.4.11.
wcag_2.1.1_keyboard-operable-all-functio: Click the browser's address bar, then press Tab repeatedly through the whole page, and note every link, button, field and other control you pass.
Compare with what you can click or drag with the pointer, and note anything the keyboard never reaches: a control, a menu item, a scrollable box, a part of a map or a custom widget.
Use each control with the keyboard: Enter or Space to activate it, arrow keys inside menus, tabs, lists and sliders, Escape to close what opens.

Where something can't be reached or used with the keyboard, check whether the page offers another way to do the same with the keyboard alone, such as previous and next buttons for a carousel. It only counts if it does everything the pointer can.
Leave out what depends on the path the pointer takes, such as freehand drawing.
Everything the page lets you do with a pointer can be done with the keyboard alone, directly or through another way that does the same job.
Something can only be done with a pointer, with no keyboard way to do the same, which fails WCAG 2.1.1.
wcag_2.1.2_no-keyboard-trap_step1: Click the address bar, then press Tab through the whole page and on into the address bar again, and Shift+Tab back.
wcag_2.1.2_no-keyboard-trap_step2: On the way, enter every part that takes focus, including embedded players, maps, editors, frames and dialogs.
wcag_2.1.2_no-keyboard-trap_step3: In each, check that Tab, Shift+Tab or Escape moves focus out again.
wcag_2.1.2_no-keyboard-trap_step4: Where it takes another key to leave, such as a text editor that uses Tab, check that the page tells you which key before or as you enter.
wcag_2.1.2_no-keyboard-trap_pass: From every part of the page, focus can be moved on with Tab, Shift+Tab or Escape, or with a key the page tells you about.
wcag_2.1.2_no-keyboard-trap_fail: Focus gets stuck in a part of the page, such as an embedded player or editor, and no key the page tells you about moves it out, which fails WCAG 2.1.2.
wcag_2.1.4_character-key-shortcuts_step1: Look in the page's help, settings and menus for keyboard shortcuts, and note those that use a single letter, number or symbol key with no Ctrl, Alt or Cmd.
wcag_2.1.4_character-key-shortcuts_step2: With focus on the page outside any field, press a few letter keys, such as j, k, s, ? and /, and note anything they do.
wcag_2.1.4_character-key-shortcuts_step3: For each such shortcut, check whether a setting turns it off or lets you change it to use Ctrl, Alt or Cmd, or whether it only works while a particular control has focus.
wcag_2.1.4_character-key-shortcuts_pass: The page has no single-key shortcuts, or each can be turned off or remapped, or works only while its control has focus.
wcag_2.1.4_character-key-shortcuts_fail: A single-key shortcut is always active and can't be turned off or remapped, so speech input or a stray key press triggers it, which fails WCAG 2.1.4.
wcag_2.2.1_time-limits-adjustable_step1: Look for anything on the page that happens after a set time: a session that ends, a form that expires, a page that refreshes or moves on by itself, content that disappears.
wcag_2.2.1_time-limits-adjustable_step2: Check the page's source and wait on it for a while to find limits that aren't announced, such as a <meta http-equiv="refresh"> or a sign-out after inactivity.
wcag_2.2.1_time-limits-adjustable_step3: For each limit, check that you can turn it off beforehand, adjust it to at least ten times its length, or are warned before it ends and can extend it with a simple action, at least ten times.
wcag_2.2.1_time-limits-adjustable_step4: Leave out limits that are part of a real-time event such as an auction, that are essential such as a timed test, or that are longer than 20 hours.
wcag_2.2.1_time-limits-adjustable_pass: Every time limit can be turned off, adjusted or extended, or is real-time, essential or over 20 hours.
wcag_2.2.1_time-limits-adjustable_fail: A time limit ends a session, a form or a page with no way to turn it off, adjust it or extend it, which fails WCAG 2.2.1.
wcag_2.2.2_auto-moving-content-pausable_: Load the page and watch for anything that moves, blinks or scrolls by itself: carousels, scrolling text, animations, background videos.
For each that starts by itself, lasts more than 5 seconds and is shown alongside other content, look for a control to pause, stop or hide it.
Check that the control can be found and used with the keyboard, and that it stops the movement rather than only slowing it.
Leave out movement that is essential, such as a progress indicator while something loads.
Everything that moves, blinks or scrolls by itself for more than 5 seconds next to other content can be paused, stopped or hidden.
Content moves, blinks or scrolls by itself for more than 5 seconds next to other content with no way to pause, stop or hide it, which fails WCAG 2.2.2.
wcag_2.2.2_auto-updating-content-control: Watch the page for content that changes by itself: news tickers, live scores, prices, feeds, timers.
For each that starts by itself and is shown alongside other content, look for a control to pause, stop or hide it, or to choose how often it updates.
Check that the control can be found and used with the keyboard.
Leave out updates that are essential to what the page is for.
Every part that updates by itself next to other content can be paused, stopped, hidden or slowed, or its updates are essential.
Content updates by itself next to other content with no way to pause, stop, hide it or change how often, which fails WCAG 2.2.2.
wcag_2.3.1_flashing-below-threshold_step: Look through the page, and play its videos and animations, for anything that flashes: a quick change between light and dark, or to and from saturated red.
For each, count the flashes in any one second, by watching it slowed down if the player allows.
Where it flashes more than three times in a second, check whether the flashing area is small (well under a quarter of the screen at a normal viewing distance) and the change in light is small.
Don't watch for long anything that flashes fast and large: stop it as soon as you have counted.
wcag_2.3.1_flashing-below-threshold_pass: Nothing flashes more than three times in any one second, or what flashes is small enough and dim enough to stay under the general and red flash thresholds.
wcag_2.3.1_flashing-below-threshold_fail: Content flashes more than three times in a second over a large area, which can cause seizures, and fails WCAG 2.3.1.
wcag_2.4.1_bypass-blocks-present_step1: Close any dialog or overlay, then note the blocks the page repeats from other pages of the site: header, navigation, search, sidebars.
wcag_2.4.1_bypass-blocks-present_step2: Click the address bar and press Tab: check whether a skip link appears that moves focus past those blocks to the main content, and follow it.
wcag_2.4.1_bypass-blocks-present_step3: Check, in the developer tools' Accessibility pane or a screen reader's lists, whether the main content is a main landmark or starts with a heading outside the navigation.
wcag_2.4.1_bypass-blocks-present_step4: Where the page has a skip link, check that its target exists and that the next Tab after following it goes into the main content.
wcag_2.4.1_bypass-blocks-present_pass: The page repeats no blocks, or a working skip link, a main landmark or headings let keyboard and screen reader users jump past them.
wcag_2.4.1_bypass-blocks-present_fail: Repeated blocks have no way to skip them, so keyboard and screen reader users must go through them on every page, which fails WCAG 2.4.1.
wcag_2.4.2_page-title-descriptive_step1: Read the page's title in the browser tab, or in <title> in the developer tools' Elements pane.
wcag_2.4.2_page-title-descriptive_step2: Check that it says what this page is about or what it is for, such as the article's headline or the step of a process ("Delivery address - Checkout - Shop").
wcag_2.4.2_page-title-descriptive_step3: Open two or three other pages of the site and check that their titles tell the pages apart, with the page's own part first.
wcag_2.4.2_page-title-descriptive_step4: Where the page changes its content without loading a new page, as a single-page app does, check that the title changes with it.
wcag_2.4.2_page-title-descriptive_pass: The page's title says what it is about or for and tells it apart from other pages.
wcag_2.4.2_page-title-descriptive_fail: The page has no title, or one that is generic, a file name, or the same as other pages', which fails WCAG 2.4.2.
wcag_2.4.4_link-purpose-clear_step1: List the page's links with a screen reader's links list, or go through them with Tab and read the Name of each in the developer tools' Accessibility pane.
wcag_2.4.4_link-purpose-clear_step2: Note links whose name doesn't say where they go or what they do: empty names, "click here", "read more", "PDF", an icon's file name.
wcag_2.4.4_link-purpose-clear_step3: For each, read the sentence, paragraph, list item or table cell the link is in, or the table header of its cell, and check whether that makes its purpose clear.
wcag_2.4.4_link-purpose-clear_step4: Check that links with the same name that lead to different places are told apart by their context.
wcag_2.4.4_link-purpose-clear_pass: Every link's purpose is clear from its name, or from its name with the sentence, paragraph, list item or table cell it is in.
wcag_2.4.4_link-purpose-clear_fail: A link has no name, or a name such as "read more" whose purpose nothing around it explains, which fails WCAG 2.4.4.
wcag_2.4.5_multiple-ways_step1: Note how you can reach this page from elsewhere in the site: the main navigation, a search, a site map, a table of contents, links between related pages.
wcag_2.4.5_multiple-ways_step2: Check that at least two of these lead to it.
wcag_2.4.5_multiple-ways_step3: Leave out a page that is a step in a process, such as the payment step of a checkout, or the result of one.
wcag_2.4.5_multiple-ways_pass: The page can be found in at least two ways, or it is a step in or the result of a process.
wcag_2.4.5_multiple-ways_fail: The page can only be reached one way, such as through the navigation alone, with no search, site map or other route, which fails WCAG 2.4.5.
wcag_2.4.6_heading-text-descriptive-evid: List the page's headings with a screen reader's headings list, or in the developer tools' Accessibility tree.
Read each heading and the content under it.
Check that each heading says what that content is about, not a placeholder, a file name or a word that could head anything.
Check that headings next to each other at the same level can be told apart.
Every heading says what the content under it is about.
A heading doesn't describe the content under it, such as "Section 1" or a file name, which fails WCAG 2.4.6.
wcag_2.4.6_form-control-label-descriptiv: Read the visible label of every field and control on the page.
Check that each says what to enter or choose, such as "Email address" rather than "Field 1" or "Text".
Where several fields share a label, such as "Name" twice, check that the page makes clear which is which, by a group heading or the rest of the label.
Every label says what its field or control is for, and fields with the same label are told apart.
A label doesn't say what its field is for, or several fields have the same label with nothing telling them apart, which fails WCAG 2.4.6.
wcag_2.4.7_focus-indicator-visible_step1: Click the address bar, then press Tab slowly through the whole page.
wcag_2.4.7_focus-indicator-visible_step2: At each stop, check that you can see which element has focus: an outline, a change of color, an underline or another visible change.
wcag_2.4.7_focus-indicator-visible_step3: Note each stop where you can't tell where focus is, and each time focus seems to disappear for a press or more.
wcag_2.4.7_focus-indicator-visible_step4: Do the same inside menus, dialogs and widgets that use the arrow keys.
wcag_2.4.7_focus-indicator-visible_pass: At every stop you can see which element has focus.
wcag_2.4.7_focus-indicator-visible_fail: Focus reaches an element with no visible change, or lands on something hidden or off screen, so keyboard users lose track of where they are, which fails WCAG 2.4.7.
wcag_2.4.11_focus-not-obscured_step1: Note what the page draws over its content: a sticky header or footer, a cookie banner, a chat button, a non-modal dialog.
wcag_2.4.11_focus-not-obscured_step2: Click the address bar and press Tab through the whole page, scrolling as the browser does.
wcag_2.4.11_focus-not-obscured_step3: At each stop, check that at least part of the focused element can be seen, not covered entirely by what the page draws over it.
wcag_2.4.11_focus-not-obscured_step4: Where something covers it, check whether you can close or move that content with the keyboard without moving focus, as for a cookie banner you can dismiss.
wcag_2.4.11_focus-not-obscured_pass: Every focused element is at least partly visible, or what covers it can be dismissed without moving focus.
wcag_2.4.11_focus-not-obscured_fail: A focused element is entirely hidden by a sticky header, a banner or other content the page puts over it, which fails WCAG 2.4.11.
wcag_2.5.1_single-pointer-alternative_st: Find the page's features that use gestures with a path or more than one finger: swiping a carousel, pinching a map to zoom, drawing a pattern, swiping a list item to delete it.
For each, look for a way to do the same with single taps or clicks: arrows for a carousel, + and - buttons for a map, a delete button.
Leave out gestures the browser or the device provide themselves, such as pinch zoom of the page, and those where the path is essential, such as a signature.
wcag_2.5.1_single-pointer-alternative_pa: Everything done with a path or multipoint gesture can also be done with single taps or clicks, or the path is essential.
wcag_2.5.1_single-pointer-alternative_fa: A feature can only be used with a swipe, a drag along a path or a multi-finger gesture, which fails WCAG 2.5.1.
wcag_2.5.2_pointer-cancellation_step1: For each kind of control on the page (buttons, links, menu items, custom controls), press the mouse button down on it and hold it without releasing.
wcag_2.5.2_pointer-cancellation_step2: Check whether anything happens on the press itself.
wcag_2.5.2_pointer-cancellation_step3: Where nothing happened yet, move the pointer off the control and release, and check that the action is cancelled.
wcag_2.5.2_pointer-cancellation_step4: Where something happens on the press, check that it can be undone, or that it is essential to act on the press, as for a piano key.
wcag_2.5.2_pointer-cancellation_pass: Actions happen on release and can be cancelled by moving off the control, or can be undone, or acting on the press is essential.
wcag_2.5.2_pointer-cancellation_fail: An action happens as soon as the pointer is pressed, with no way to cancel or undo it, which fails WCAG 2.5.2.
wcag_2.5.3_label-in-name_step1: Find every control with a visible label made of text: buttons, links, fields, tabs, menu items, and controls labelled by text next to them.
wcag_2.5.3_label-in-name_step2: For each, read its Name in the developer tools' Accessibility pane.
wcag_2.5.3_label-in-name_step3: Check that the name contains the visible label's words, in the same order, ideally at the start (a button showing "Send" named "Send message", not "Submit").
wcag_2.5.3_label-in-name_step4: Leave out a label made only of symbols, such as "×" or ">": the name should say what it does.
wcag_2.5.3_label-in-name_pass: Every control's name contains the words of its visible label, in order.
wcag_2.5.3_label-in-name_fail: A control's name doesn't contain its visible label, so someone who uses speech input can't activate it by saying what they see, which fails WCAG 2.5.3.
wcag_2.5.4_motion-actuation_step1: Find the page's features that respond to moving or tilting the device, or to gestures in front of a camera: shake to undo, tilt to scroll, turn to steer.
wcag_2.5.4_motion-actuation_step2: On a phone or tablet, try them, or read the page's help to find them.
wcag_2.5.4_motion-actuation_step3: For each, check that a control on the page does the same, and that a setting turns the motion response off so the device can be moved by accident.
wcag_2.5.4_motion-actuation_step4: Leave out motion that is essential, such as a step counter.
wcag_2.5.4_motion-actuation_pass: The page uses no device motion, or each motion feature has a control that does the same and can be turned off.
wcag_2.5.4_motion-actuation_fail: A feature can only be used by moving the device, or its response to motion can't be turned off, which fails WCAG 2.5.4.
wcag_2.5.7_dragging-alternative_step1: Find the page's features that use dragging: sliders, lists you reorder, files you drop, items you move between columns, a map you pan.
wcag_2.5.7_dragging-alternative_step2: For each, look for a way to do the same with single taps or clicks: clicking a point on a slider's track, up and down buttons, a menu to move an item, arrow buttons on a map.
wcag_2.5.7_dragging-alternative_step3: Leave out dragging that is essential, such as drawing a signature.
wcag_2.5.7_dragging-alternative_pass: Everything done by dragging can also be done with single taps or clicks, or dragging is essential.
wcag_2.5.7_dragging-alternative_fail: A feature can only be used by dragging, which fails WCAG 2.5.7.
wcag_2.5.8_target-size-minimum-pointer_s: Look for small controls: icons, close buttons, pagination, links in a row, small check boxes.
Inspect each and read its size in the developer tools' box model: check that it is at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels.
Where it is smaller, check whether a 24-pixel circle centred on it would touch another target, or the circle of another small target.
Leave out links in a sentence or paragraph, controls the browser draws unstyled, controls with a full-size equivalent elsewhere on the page, and targets whose size is essential, such as a map's pins.
wcag_2.5.8_target-size-minimum-pointer_p: Every target is at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, or far enough from others, or one of the exceptions.
wcag_2.5.8_target-size-minimum-pointer_f: A target smaller than 24 by 24 CSS pixels sits so close to another that their 24-pixel circles overlap, with no exception that applies, which fails WCAG 2.5.8.
wcag_3.1.1_page-language-correct_step1: Read the lang attribute of the <html> element in the developer tools' Elements pane.
wcag_3.1.1_page-language-correct_step2: Check that it is a language code (en, fr, pt-BR) and that it is the language most of the page's text is in.
wcag_3.1.1_page-language-correct_step3: Where <html> also has xml:lang, check that both give the same language.
wcag_3.1.1_page-language-correct_pass: The <html> element's lang gives the language most of the page is in.
wcag_3.1.1_page-language-correct_fail: The page has no lang, a wrong or invalid one, so screen readers read it with the wrong voice and pronunciation, which fails WCAG 3.1.1.
wcag_3.1.2_parts-language-marked_step1: Read through the page and note passages, quotes, phrases and names of things written in another language than the page's, including a language picker's options.
wcag_3.1.2_parts-language-marked_step2: For each, check in the developer tools' Elements pane that it, or an element around it, has a lang attribute with that language's code.
wcag_3.1.2_parts-language-marked_step3: Leave out proper names, technical terms, and words that have become part of the page's language, such as "café" in English.
wcag_3.1.2_parts-language-marked_step4: Listen to a few with a screen reader to check it switches pronunciation.
wcag_3.1.2_parts-language-marked_pass: Every passage or phrase in another language is marked with a valid lang attribute for that language.
wcag_3.1.2_parts-language-marked_fail: A passage or phrase in another language isn't marked with its language, or is marked with a wrong code, so it is read with the wrong pronunciation, which fails WCAG 3.1.2.
wcag_3.2.1_focus-no-change-of-context_st: Click the address bar, then press Tab through the whole page, without pressing Enter or Space.

At each stop, check that nothing changes just because the element got focus: no new page or window opens, no form is sent, focus isn't moved elsewhere, and the content doesn't change in a way that changes what the page is.
wcag_3.2.1_focus-no-change-of-context_pa: Moving focus never, by itself, opens a page or window, sends a form, moves focus or changes the content's meaning.
wcag_3.2.1_focus-no-change-of-context_fa: An element changes the context as soon as it gets focus, such as opening a new window or sending a form, which fails WCAG 3.2.1.
wcag_3.2.2_input-no-unexpected-change_st: Find every field, check box, radio button and drop-down on the page.
With the keyboard, change each value: type in it, tick it, or move through a drop-down's options with the arrow keys, without pressing Enter or a button.
Check that changing a value doesn't, by itself, send a form, load another page, open a window or move focus elsewhere.
Where it does, check that text before the control says it will happen.
wcag_3.2.2_input-no-unexpected-change_pa: Changing a value never changes the context by itself, or the page says beforehand that it will.
wcag_3.2.2_input-no-unexpected-change_fa: Changing a value, such as picking from a drop-down, loads a new page, sends the form or moves focus without warning, which fails WCAG 3.2.2.
wcag_3.2.3_navigation-consistent_step1: Note the blocks of links the page shares with others in the site: main navigation, header and footer links, a sidebar menu, a search.
wcag_3.2.3_navigation-consistent_step2: Open three or four other pages of the site, of different kinds.
wcag_3.2.3_navigation-consistent_step3: Check that these blocks, and the links in them, come in the same order relative to each other on every page, even where some pages add or leave out links.
wcag_3.2.3_navigation-consistent_step4: Leave out changes the user made, such as reordering a menu.
wcag_3.2.3_navigation-consistent_pass: Navigation repeated across pages comes in the same relative order on each.
wcag_3.2.3_navigation-consistent_fail: Repeated navigation changes order from page to page, which fails WCAG 3.2.3.
wcag_3.2.4_identification-consistent_ste: Note the controls and icons the page shares with others in the site: search, sign in, print, download, cart, share, next and previous.
Open three or four other pages of the site.
Check that each control that does the same thing has the same label, icon and text alternative on each page ("Search" everywhere, not "Search" on one and "Find" on another).
wcag_3.2.4_identification-consistent_pas: Each component that does the same thing across the site is labelled the same way.
wcag_3.2.4_identification-consistent_fai: A component that does the same thing is labelled differently on different pages, which fails WCAG 3.2.4.
wcag_3.2.6_help-consistent_step1: Find the help the page offers: contact details, a contact form, a chat, a help or FAQ link.
wcag_3.2.6_help-consistent_step2: Open three or four other pages of the site that offer it.
wcag_3.2.6_help-consistent_step3: Check that each form of help is in the same place relative to the rest of the page content on each, such as always last in the header.
wcag_3.2.6_help-consistent_pass: The site offers no help, or each form of help it offers on several pages is in the same relative place on each.
wcag_3.2.6_help-consistent_fail: Help offered on several pages moves from one place to another, which fails WCAG 3.2.6.
wcag_3.3.1_errors-identified_step1: Find each form on the page and send it empty, then with wrong values: a malformed email, letters in a number field, a date in the past.
wcag_3.3.1_errors-identified_step2: Check that each error the page detects is shown in text, not only by color or an icon, next to the field or in a list at the top.
wcag_3.3.1_errors-identified_step3: Check that the text says which field is wrong and what is wrong with it.
wcag_3.3.1_errors-identified_step4: Check with a screen reader that the error is announced or reached easily, and that each wrong field is marked invalid.
wcag_3.3.1_errors-identified_pass: Every input error the page detects is shown in text that names the field and the problem.
wcag_3.3.1_errors-identified_fail: An input error is shown only by color or an icon, not at all, or without saying which field is wrong, which fails WCAG 3.3.1.
wcag_3.3.2_labels-instructions-provided_: Find every field and control that asks for input on the page.
Check that each has a label you can see without hovering or typing: not only a placeholder that disappears when you type, or a title shown on hover.
Where the input must follow rules, such as a date format, a password's requirements or which fields are required, check that the page says so before the user sends it.
Check in the developer tools' Accessibility pane that each field has one name, from its label.
Every field has a visible label, and the page gives the instructions the input needs before it is sent.
A field has no visible label, only a placeholder or a hover title, or input rules are given only after an error, which fails WCAG 3.3.2.
wcag_3.3.3_error-suggestions_step1: Send each form with wrong values: a malformed email, a date in the wrong format, a value out of range, a password that breaks the rules.
wcag_3.3.3_error-suggestions_step2: For each error, read the message and check whether it says how to fix it, such as the expected format or the allowed range, where the page knows.
wcag_3.3.3_error-suggestions_step3: Leave out errors where saying how would put security at risk or defeat the purpose, such as a wrong password or the answer to a test.
wcag_3.3.3_error-suggestions_pass: Every error message says how to fix the input where the page knows how and saying so is safe.
wcag_3.3.3_error-suggestions_fail: An error message says only that the input is wrong when the page knows how to fix it, such as "Invalid date" without the expected format, which fails WCAG 3.3.3.
wcag_3.3.4_submission-reversible-checked: Find the page's forms that make a commitment or change data: orders, payments, bookings, contracts, test answers, deleting or changing an account's data.
Go through each up to the last step (with test data, stopping before any real commitment).

Check that at least one of these holds: you can cancel or undo it afterwards; the page checks the input and lets you correct it; or the page shows what you entered and asks you to confirm before it is sent.
Each such submission can be reversed, is checked with a chance to correct it, or is reviewed and confirmed before it is final.
A submission with legal or financial effect, or that changes stored data, is final at once, with no check, review or undo, which fails WCAG 3.3.4.
wcag_3.3.7_redundant-entry_step1: Go through each process on the page that has several steps, such as a checkout, an application or a registration.
wcag_3.3.7_redundant-entry_step2: Note each time a step asks for something you already entered in an earlier step, such as an address or a name.
wcag_3.3.7_redundant-entry_step3: Check that it is filled in for you, or offered to pick ("same as delivery address").
wcag_3.3.7_redundant-entry_step4: Leave out re-entry that is essential, such as typing a new password twice, or needed for security.
wcag_3.3.7_redundant-entry_pass: Nothing entered earlier in a process is asked for again, or it is filled in or offered, or re-entering it is essential.
wcag_3.3.7_redundant-entry_fail: A step asks the user to type again information they already gave in the same process, which fails WCAG 3.3.7.
wcag_3.3.8_authentication-no-cognitive-t: Go through each way the site lets you sign in or verify yourself, with a test account.
Note each step that asks you to remember something (a password), transcribe it (a code from another device), or solve something (a puzzle, a calculation, picking images).
For a password or code, check that you can paste it and that a password manager can fill it, so it needn't be remembered or retyped.
For other tests, check that another method is offered, or that the test only asks to recognize objects or something you gave the site.
Every sign-in step that asks to remember, transcribe or solve something allows pasting and password managers, or offers another way, or only asks to recognize objects or your own content.
Signing in requires remembering, transcribing or solving something with no way around it, such as a code field that blocks pasting, which fails WCAG 3.3.8.
wcag_4.1.1_id-unique-page-wide_step1: In the developer tools' Console, list repeated ids with: [...document.querySelectorAll('[id]')].map(e => e.id).filter((id, i, all) => all.indexOf(id) !== i)
wcag_4.1.1_id-unique-page-wide_step2: For each repeated id, check whether a label, an ARIA attribute or a script refers to it, and whether the element it means is the first one with that id.
wcag_4.1.1_id-unique-page-wide_step3: Check what a screen reader says for the controls that use those ids.
wcag_4.1.1_id-unique-page-wide_pass: Every id is unique in its document, or a repeated id is never referred to.
wcag_4.1.1_id-unique-page-wide_fail: Repeated ids make a label, an ARIA relationship or a control point at the wrong element, which fails WCAG 4.1.1 under WCAG 2.0 and 2.1. WCAG 2.2 treats 4.1.1 as always met: there the effect fails 1.3.1 or 4.1.2.
wcag_4.1.2_components-named_step1: Go through every link, button, field, frame and custom control on the page, by pressing Tab and inside widgets with the arrow keys.
wcag_4.1.2_components-named_step2: For each, read the Name in the developer tools' Accessibility pane, or listen to what a screen reader says.
wcag_4.1.2_components-named_step3: Check that each has a name that says what it is for, including icon-only buttons, frames ("Video player", "Map") and dialogs.
wcag_4.1.2_components-named_step4: Check that frames with the same name show the same thing, and that names given only for braille have a spoken equivalent.
wcag_4.1.2_components-named_pass: Every link, control, frame and dialog has a name that says what it is for.
wcag_4.1.2_components-named_fail: A link, control, frame or dialog has no name, or one that doesn't say what it is for, so assistive technology announces only its role, which fails WCAG 4.1.2.
wcag_4.1.2_roles-match-behavior_step1: For each control on the page, note what it does when used: opens a page (a link), acts on the page (a button), toggles (a check box or switch), opens a list (a menu or combo box).
wcag_4.1.2_roles-match-behavior_step2: Read its Role in the developer tools' Accessibility pane, or listen to a screen reader, and check that the role matches what it does.
wcag_4.1.2_roles-match-behavior_step3: Pay attention to custom controls built from divs and spans, links used as buttons and buttons used as links.
wcag_4.1.2_roles-match-behavior_step4: Check that no control holds another one inside it, such as a button inside a link, and that controls whose children are presentational, such as a tab or a button, hold nothing focusable.
wcag_4.1.2_roles-match-behavior_pass: Every control's role says what it does, and no control is nested inside another.
wcag_4.1.2_roles-match-behavior_fail: A control has no role, a wrong one (a clickable div with no role, a link that acts as a button), or holds another control inside it, which fails WCAG 4.1.2.
wcag_4.1.2_states-values-exposed_step1: Find the controls that have a state or value: check boxes, switches, radio buttons, expandable sections and menus, tabs, sliders, selected items, pressed buttons.
wcag_4.1.2_states-values-exposed_step2: Read each one's state and value in the developer tools' Accessibility pane, or listen with a screen reader: checked, expanded, selected, pressed, current value.
wcag_4.1.2_states-values-exposed_step3: Change each with the keyboard and check that the state or value read changes with what you see.
wcag_4.1.2_states-values-exposed_step4: For an expandable control, check that it says expanded only while what it opens is shown.
wcag_4.1.2_states-values-exposed_pass: Every control's state and value are exposed and change with what is on screen.
wcag_4.1.2_states-values-exposed_fail: A control's state or value isn't exposed, or doesn't change when it changes on screen, such as a custom check box always read as not checked, which fails WCAG 4.1.2.
wcag_4.1.2_aria-used-validly_step1: In the developer tools' Elements pane, search the markup for aria- and role= and look at each use.
wcag_4.1.2_aria-used-validly_step2: Check that each aria-* attribute is a real one, has a valid value, and is allowed on its element's role.
wcag_4.1.2_aria-used-validly_step3: Check that ids that aria-labelledby, aria-describedby, aria-controls and the like point to exist once each.
wcag_4.1.2_aria-used-validly_step4: Check that nothing that takes focus is inside an element with aria-hidden="true", and that <body> isn't hidden.
wcag_4.1.2_aria-used-validly_pass: ARIA attributes are real, valid and allowed where they are, their ids are unique, and nothing focusable is hidden.
wcag_4.1.2_aria-used-validly_fail: An ARIA attribute is misspelt, has an invalid value or is not allowed on its role, an id it points to is missing or repeated, or something focusable is hidden from assistive technology, which fails WCAG 4.1.2.
wcag_4.1.3_status-messages-announced_ste: Find the messages the page shows without moving focus: "Added to cart", search result counts, "Saved", progress, form errors listed after sending.
Turn on a screen reader and cause each message, by the action that shows it.
Check that the screen reader says the message without focus moving to it.
Where it says nothing, check in the developer tools that the message is in an element with role="status", role="alert" or aria-live, present before the message arrives and not hidden.
wcag_4.1.3_status-messages-announced_pas: Every status message is announced by a screen reader without focus moving to it.
wcag_4.1.3_status-messages-announced_fai: A status message appears on screen but a screen reader doesn't say it, which fails WCAG 4.1.3.
wcag_1.2.6_sign-language_step1: Find every prerecorded video with sound on the page.
wcag_1.2.6_sign-language_step2: Play each and look for a sign language interpreter in the picture, or a choice in the player or next to it that shows a signed version.
wcag_1.2.6_sign-language_step3: Check that the signing covers the whole of what is said and the sounds that matter, and is large enough to follow.
wcag_1.2.6_sign-language_step4: Leave out a video that is itself an alternative for text on the page and is labelled as such.
wcag_1.2.6_sign-language_pass: Every prerecorded video with sound has sign language interpretation of all its speech and important sounds.
wcag_1.2.6_sign-language_fail: A prerecorded video with sound has no sign language interpretation, which fails WCAG 1.2.6.
wcag_1.2.7_extended-audio-description_st: Find every prerecorded video with sound whose picture shows information the sound doesn't say.
Play its audio description, and note where the description can't fit in the pauses of the speech, so that something shown goes undescribed.
Check that a version is offered where the video pauses to let the description say everything shown.
wcag_1.2.7_extended-audio-description_pa: Every video whose pauses are too short for a full description has an extended audio description that stops the video to give it.
wcag_1.2.7_extended-audio-description_fa: A video's audio description leaves out what is shown because the pauses are too short, and no extended version is offered, which fails WCAG 1.2.7.
wcag_1.2.8_media-text-alternative_step1: Find every prerecorded video on the page, with or without sound.
wcag_1.2.8_media-text-alternative_step2: Look next to each for a text alternative: a transcript that describes what is shown as well as what is said and heard.
wcag_1.2.8_media-text-alternative_step3: Watch the video and compare: the text should tell the whole story, including actions, scene changes and text on screen.
wcag_1.2.8_media-text-alternative_pass: Every prerecorded video has a full text alternative next to it that gives everything it shows and says.
wcag_1.2.8_media-text-alternative_fail: A prerecorded video has no text alternative, or one that gives only the speech, which fails WCAG 1.2.8.
wcag_1.2.9_live-audio-alternative_step1: Find any live audio without video on the page: a radio stream, a live podcast, an audio conference.
wcag_1.2.9_live-audio-alternative_step2: While it is live, look for a text alternative shown with it: live captions, a live transcript, or the script it follows.
wcag_1.2.9_live-audio-alternative_step3: Check that the text follows what is said and the sounds that matter.
wcag_1.2.9_live-audio-alternative_pass: The page has no live audio-only content, or it comes with a live text alternative.
wcag_1.2.9_live-audio-alternative_fail: Live audio-only content has no text alternative, which fails WCAG 1.2.9.
wcag_1.3.6_purpose-identified_step1: Check in the developer tools' Accessibility tree that each region of the page (header, navigation, main content, search, footer) is a landmark.
wcag_1.3.6_purpose-identified_step2: For icons and controls with a common purpose (home, search, help, close, next), check that the markup names that purpose: in the element's name, its role, or attributes for that purpose.
wcag_1.3.6_purpose-identified_step3: For fields about the user, check that autocomplete gives their purpose.
wcag_1.3.6_purpose-identified_pass: Regions, icons and controls with a common purpose have it in the markup, so tools can show them in a way the user prefers.
wcag_1.3.6_purpose-identified_fail: A region, icon or control's purpose is given only by its look, which fails WCAG 1.3.6.
wcag_1.4.6_contrast-enhanced-text_step1: Look through the page for text that seems faint against its background, as for 1.4.3.
wcag_1.4.6_contrast-enhanced-text_step2: For each, inspect it and click the swatch of its color in the developer tools' Styles pane: the picker shows its contrast ratio.
wcag_1.4.6_contrast-enhanced-text_step3: Where the background is an image, a gradient or a semi-transparent layer, measure the text against the part of the background where it is least visible, with a color contrast checker.
wcag_1.4.6_contrast-enhanced-text_step4: Check the ratio is at least 7:1, or 4.5:1 for large text: at least 24 pixels (18pt), or 18.66 pixels (14pt) and bold.
wcag_1.4.6_contrast-enhanced-text_step5: Leave out text in logos, on disabled controls, and text that is only decoration.
wcag_1.4.6_contrast-enhanced-text_pass: All text and images of text have a contrast of at least 7:1 with their background, or 4.5:1 when large.
wcag_1.4.6_contrast-enhanced-text_fail: Text has less contrast with its background than 7:1 (4.5:1 for large text), which fails WCAG 1.4.6.
wcag_1.4.7_background-audio-low_step1: Find prerecorded audio that is mostly speech: podcasts, narrated videos, interviews.
wcag_1.4.7_background-audio-low_step2: Listen for background sound behind the speech: music, noise, effects.
wcag_1.4.7_background-audio-low_step3: Where there is some, check whether it can be turned off, or is clearly much quieter than the speech (about four times quieter), except for short occasional sounds.
wcag_1.4.7_background-audio-low_step4: Leave out music, singing, sound logos and CAPTCHAs.
wcag_1.4.7_background-audio-low_pass: Speech has no background sound, or it can be turned off, or it is about four times quieter than the speech.
wcag_1.4.7_background-audio-low_fail: Background sound behind speech is loud enough to make the speech hard to follow and can't be turned off, which fails WCAG 1.4.7.
wcag_1.4.8_visual-presentation_step1: Find the page's blocks of text: paragraphs of an article, long descriptions.
wcag_1.4.8_visual-presentation_step2: Check that a line holds at most about 80 characters (40 for Chinese, Japanese or Korean), and that the text is not justified to both edges.
wcag_1.4.8_visual-presentation_step3: Check that lines are spaced at least 1.5 and paragraphs further apart, or that the page offers a setting for it.
wcag_1.4.8_visual-presentation_step4: Turn on a high-contrast theme or change the browser's colors, and check that the text takes them, or that the page offers its own color choice.
wcag_1.4.8_visual-presentation_step5: Zoom the text to 200% and check that it can be read without scrolling sideways in a window the full width of the screen.
wcag_1.4.8_visual-presentation_pass: Blocks of text meet each of the five conditions, directly or through a setting the page offers.
wcag_1.4.8_visual-presentation_fail: A block of text is wider than 80 characters, justified, tightly spaced, can't take the user's colors, or needs sideways scrolling at 200%, which fails WCAG 1.4.8.
wcag_1.4.9_no-images-of-text_step1: Look for images that contain words, including logos and banners.
wcag_1.4.9_no-images-of-text_step2: Try to select their words with the pointer, or inspect them, to tell images of text from real text.
wcag_1.4.9_no-images-of-text_step3: Check that each image of text is pure decoration, or a logo or brand name, or a case where the exact look of the text is essential.
wcag_1.4.9_no-images-of-text_pass: Images of text are only decoration, logos, or where their look is essential.
wcag_1.4.9_no-images-of-text_fail: Words are shown as an image where the look isn't essential, which fails WCAG 1.4.9.
wcag_2.1.3_keyboard-no-exception_step1: Do the walk-through of 2.1.1: press Tab through the whole page and use every control with the keyboard alone.
wcag_2.1.3_keyboard-no-exception_step2: This time include what depends on the pointer's path, such as drawing, a signature or a freehand selection, and check that the keyboard can do it too.
wcag_2.1.3_keyboard-no-exception_step3: Check that scrollable areas, mouse-only handlers and clickable elements can all be reached and used with the keyboard.
wcag_2.1.3_keyboard-no-exception_pass: Everything the page lets you do with a pointer can be done with the keyboard alone, with no exception.
wcag_2.1.3_keyboard-no-exception_fail: Something can only be done with a pointer, even where it depends on the pointer's path, which fails WCAG 2.1.3.
wcag_2.2.3_no-timing_step1: Look for anything with a time limit, as for 2.2.1: sessions that end, forms that expire, content that moves on, tests with a clock.
wcag_2.2.3_no-timing_step2: Check that none has a limit, even one that can be extended.
wcag_2.2.3_no-timing_step3: Leave out non-interactive synchronized media, such as a video, and real-time events, such as an auction.
wcag_2.2.3_no-timing_pass: Nothing on the page is timed, apart from non-interactive media and real-time events.
wcag_2.2.3_no-timing_fail: An interaction has a time limit, even an adjustable one, which fails WCAG 2.2.3.
wcag_2.2.4_interruptions-postponable_ste: Note what interrupts you while you use the page: pop-ups, notifications, chat invitations, content that refreshes or updates by itself, a page that reloads.
Look in the page and its settings for a way to postpone or turn off each.
Leave out interruptions about an emergency.
wcag_2.2.4_interruptions-postponable_pas: Every interruption can be postponed or turned off, or is about an emergency.
wcag_2.2.4_interruptions-postponable_fai: The page interrupts with updates, alerts or a refresh that can't be postponed or turned off, which fails WCAG 2.2.4.
wcag_2.2.5_reauthentication-keeps-data_s: Sign in with a test account and start a task that takes several steps, such as a long form.
Let the session expire, or wait until it does, while the task is half done.
Sign in again and check that you come back to where you were, with what you had entered.
wcag_2.2.5_reauthentication-keeps-data_p: After signing in again, the task continues with nothing lost.
wcag_2.2.5_reauthentication-keeps-data_f: When a session expires, what the user had entered is lost, which fails WCAG 2.2.5.
wcag_2.2.6_timeout-warning_step1: Find the tasks where leaving the page idle could lose what you entered: forms, carts, bookings.
wcag_2.2.6_timeout-warning_step2: Check that, at the start of the task, the page says how long it keeps data while you are inactive.
wcag_2.2.6_timeout-warning_step3: Leave out data kept for more than 20 hours.
wcag_2.2.6_timeout-warning_pass: The page warns how long inactivity may lose data, or keeps it for more than 20 hours.
wcag_2.2.6_timeout-warning_fail: Inactivity can lose the user's data without the page having said how long it allows, which fails WCAG 2.2.6.
wcag_2.3.2_no-flashing_step1: Look through the page, and play its videos and animations, for anything that flashes.
wcag_2.3.2_no-flashing_step2: For each, count the flashes in any one second; stop it as soon as you have counted if it flashes fast.
wcag_2.3.2_no-flashing_step3: Unlike 2.3.1, no size or brightness exception applies.
wcag_2.3.2_no-flashing_pass: Nothing flashes more than three times in any one second.
wcag_2.3.2_no-flashing_fail: Something flashes more than three times in a second, however small, which fails WCAG 2.3.2.
wcag_2.3.3_motion-animation-disableable_: Use the page and note motion caused by what you do: parallax when scrolling, zooming or sliding transitions, elements that move as the pointer moves.
Turn on reduced motion (in the operating system, or in the developer tools' Rendering pane, emulate prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) and reload.
Check that this motion stops, or that the page offers its own setting to turn it off.
Leave out motion that is essential to what is shown.
Motion caused by interaction stops with reduced motion or a setting on the page, or is essential.
Motion caused by interaction, such as parallax scrolling, can't be turned off, which fails WCAG 2.3.3.
